subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Labour) moved:
subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
That Bill C-85, an Act to provide for the resumption and continuance of railway operations and for the settlement of disputes respecting terms and conditions of employment between railway companies and their employees, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on second reading of the Bill now before the House, namely, the Maintenance of Railway Operations Act, 1987. The purpose of the Bill is, above all, to order a resumption of rail traffic so vital to the nation's economy.
August 27, 1987

As Hon. Members will be aware, four separate labour disputes involving the major national railway companies and unions representing their employees have recently reached a critical stage. One of these disputes has now culminated in a national rail strike.
The four disputes comprise the Associated Railway Unions which represent some 48,000 railway workers in nine separate unions who negotiate jointly with the Canadian National Railway Company and CP Rail; two smaller groups of railway shopcraft employees represented by member unions of the Canadian Council of Railway Shopcraft Unions which is negotiating separately with each of the two companies, and the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers negotiating separately on behalf of its members employed by Canadian National.
It is perhaps obvious but nevertheless important to point out that this Bill would not have been necessary had the parties to the railway disputes been capable of meeting their responsibilities under the Canada Labour Code, Part V by renewing their collective agreements.
Despite considerable conciliation assistance provided to them by the Government, they were unable to do so without a work stoppage. This work stoppage, principally involving a strike declared by the Associated Railway Unions at midnight on Sunday, August 23, has paralyzed rail transportation and brought key sectors of the Canadian economy into jeopardy. As I advised the parties in a telegram on August 24, the Government cannot, and will not, tolerate a shutdown of the nation's major transportation systems.
I have concluded that there is no reasonable prospect for a negotiated settlement to the current work stoppage. Therefore, I have absolutely no hesitation in introducing the present Bill into the House.
In addition to ordering a resumption of work, the Bill provides for a means of settling the labour disputes between the parties. However, before dealing in more detail with the provisions of the Bill, I would like to emphasize to Hon. Members certain factors which have convinced the Government that rapid and decisive action is required to terminate the current strike and to restore rail services to the Canadian public and the national economy.

Other than Canada, there are few countries in the world where economic and social history rests so heavily on rail transportation. The establishment of the rail link was an enormous contribution to the development and expansion of this country in the last century, Madam Speaker, and in more recent times it has enabled Canada to rank among the world's major trading nations.
The railways built Canada in times past and they continue to be its economic mainstay.
Maintenance of Railway Operations

Despite significant advances in other modes of transportation, notably by road and water, Canada's railways still account for close to 40 per cent of all freight tonnage moved in this country. More importantly, the producers of some commodities are virtually tied to rail transportation in order to move their products to markets economically. Western grain farmers present an obvious example of primary producers who rely heavily on the railways as part of an integrated transportation network to carry their crops efficiently from the prairie elevators to domestic and foreign customers.
This Government has previously demonstrated its commitment to western farmers. This highly productive group faces uncertain and extremely competitive world markets. It does not deserve to have additional obstacles placed in its way.
The producers of other bulk products in western Canada and in other regions are also seriously affected by the disruption of rail traffic. Manufacturers, exporters, importers and just about every sector of the economy is in some significant way harmed by a cessation of rail services. Increasingly, commuters in our large urban centres have come to rely on rail passenger services to take them to and from their place of work.
In addition to the direct impact of the halting of railway transportation, there is immeasurable harm resulting from the so-called ripple effect of a rail strike. Industries which cannot obtain parts or ship their goods are required to shut down production and lay-off employees. It is this ripple effect of a rail strike which is perhaps the most damaging to the over-all economy. The longer a strike lasts, the more far reaching the impact on Canadians throughout the country.
Via Rail employees, who have renewed their collective agreements without work stoppages, have already been subject to lay-off. Seafarers on the Great Lakes system and in our coastal waters could be among the next groups to feel the effect as rail shipments cease to arrive at or depart from our ports and harbours. Longshoremen and other port workers will be similarly affected.
It may take somewhat longer for the impact to be felt in other areas of trade and commerce. However, the effect would inevitably spread throughout the production and distribution chain if a work stoppage is allowed to continue.

Madam Speaker, this Government has invested too much effort to build a solid foundation for sustained economic recovery to let Canadian workers, Canadian producers and Canadian businessmen be the victims of the consequences of a lengthy breakdown of rail transport services.
It should therefore come as no surprise, Madam Speaker, to the parties concerned in the railway dispute, the Members of this House and the Canadian people that this Government decided to act quickly and table this Bill in the House, in order to put an end to a work stoppage that might prove disastrous.

August 27, 1987
Maintenance of Railway Operations
It is only the fourth time in about 37 years that Parliament is being asked to put an end to a railway work stoppage. The last time was in August, 1973, exactly 14 years ago. At the time, Madam Speaker, despite numerous efforts to help the parties settle their differences, rotating strikes went on for nearly a month before they turned into a general work stoppage. After seven days during which the economy of this country suffered increasingly serious losses, the House was asked to intervene. This time, the Government did not wait that long. There were some local walk-outs in the Montreal and Toronto areas last week and also in Sarnia. A general strike was called to which we must put a stop.
Although we are acting quickly, Madam Speaker, one could hardly call our action precipitous. The parties had every opportunity to settle their differences and received all necessary help to that end.
[ English]
In the Associated Railway Unions dispute, the previous collective agreements expired on December 31, 1986. Following notices of dispute filed by the parties in January of this year, a conciliation officer was appointed who endeavoured to assist the parties in the resolution of the dispute. Despite the officer's efforts, no settlement was achieved. On March 4, I appointed Mr. Douglas C. Stanley as conciliation commissioner. In the ensuing months Mr. Stanley met with the parties in an effort to conciliate their differences. As was the case at the conciliation officer stage, Commissioner Stanley was unable to assist the parties to resolve their differences and he proceeded to write his report and recommendations.
On August 10, 1 released Mr. Stanley's report to the parties, as 1 am required to do under the provisions of the Canada Labour Code. The report was subsequently made available generally and I am sure those Members who have read the report will have found it comprehensive. It was definitive with respect to wages, rejecting the positions of both parties, and instead recommending a settlement package already agreed to in other segments of the railway industry, such as Via Rail and the Ontario Northland Railway.
In recommending two annual increases at 3 per cent in a two-year contract, the commissioner commented that such a settlement was not unreasonable in relation to wage settlements being achieved in free collective bargaining. He was similarly definitive in other wage-related areas, rejecting the concept of a two-tier wage scale as demanded by the companies and recommending an increase in the night shift differential.
In other areas, notably contracting out and employment security, the commissioner was less definitive. Nevertheless, he suggested certain constructive avenues for pursuing the compromises and trade-offs required for settlement.
The initial reactions of the parties to the commissioner's report were encouraging. Reports indicated they regarded Mr. Stanley's recommendations as a useful basis for further
negotiations. While the reported statements were guarded in some respects, it was reasonable to conclude that the parties found the commissioner's recommendations to offer a good framework for a possible agreement. These encouraging signs were enhanced when, on August 13, 1 was sent a joint request for a mediation assistance signed by the chairman of the Associated Railway Unions and the vice-presidents of the two railway companies responsible for labour relations.
1 responded willingly to this request and on August 14 I appointed Mr. M. K. Carson, an industrial relations consultant, as mediator, pursuant to Section 195 of the Canada Labour Code. Mac Carson is a veteran of railway labour negotiations. A former railway employee and trade union official, he has some 15 years experience with the federal mediation and conciliation service and is well respected by the parties in this dispute.
Mr. Carson commenced his mediation meetings in Montreal on Monday, August 17, and worked constantly with the parties throughout last week. Although significant progress was made earlier in the week, it became clear on Saturday, August 22 that a settlement would still escape the parties prior to the expiry of a strike deadline set by the unions for midnight on August 23. Mr. Carson regretfully adjourned the mediation meetings and returned to Ottawa.

As my colleagues would know, Madam Speaker, the moment the strike was called on Monday I sent a telegram to the parties to convene their bargaining committees for a last attempt at mediation. Besides again offering Mr. Carson's services to the parties, 1 asked my Labour Associate Deputy Minister Bill Kelly to take part in the negotiations. Madam Speaker, 1 should think there is no need to remind Hon. Members that Mr. Kelly is fully conversant with railway issues and very well known as the federal Government's chief negotiator.
Mr. Kelly and Mr. Carson met with the parties in Hull on August 25, 26 and 27. This week Mr. Kelly led the mediation talks in his own characteristic way, keeping labour and management negotiators working hard through the night on Tuesday, late Wednesday night, and again today. Every single option likely to lead to a settlement was explored during the sustained and exhaustive mediation talks.
Madam Speaker, notwithstanding the urgency of the situation, the parties were unable to benefit from this ultimate opportunity to settle their differences and put an end to their conflict.

The conciliation and mediation activities to which I have been referring relate to the main dispute involving the Associated Railway Unions and both national railway companies. This dispute now involves a national strike. As I indicated earlier, there are other labour disputes currently
August 27, 1987

affecting the railways. As in the case of the ARU, these other disputes involve renewals of collective agreements which expired on December 31, 1986.
While the ARU includes trade unions representing a large number of railway shopcraft employees, some shopcraft unions are negotiating separately with Canadian National and CP Rail under the auspices of the Canadian Council of Railway Shopcraft Unions. The Council has three member unions negotiating with Canadian National and five member unions negotiating with CP Rail.
Conciliation officer appointments were also made in January in these disputes. Again, no settlements were forthcoming at the officer stage and 1 appointed Douglas Stanley as Conciliation Commissioner in each of the disputes on March 4, 1987, the same date as his appointment in the ARU case. Mr. Stanley was not able to conciliate the disputes and I released his separate reports to the parties on Monday, August 17, with general release taking place the following day.
While the unions and the council have now acquired strike rights, they have not exercised them. Their members are now subject to lay-off as a result of the shutdown of railway operations.
A fourth dispute involves the International Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers. While the brotherhood is negotiating as part of the ARU with CP Rail it has opted to negotiate separately on behalf of some 2,600 members employed by Canadian National. Again, the collective agreement in this dispute expired on December 31 last year.
A conciliation officer appointment was made last February and a dispute remained at that stage until Monday last, August 24, when the parties were informed that I would not be appointing a conciliation commissioner. The parties will acquire strike and lock-out rights at midnight on August 31.
1 have made this brief review of the status of the other current railway labour disputes because it is very relevant to the Bill currently before the House. The Maintenance of Railways Operations Act, 1987 has been drafted with separate parts applicable to each of the four disputes concerned.
In the case of the Associated Railway Unions, the appropriate part would come into force on the day following that on which the Bill is assented to. The other parts would come into force on days and times to be fixed by proclamation. I intend to explain this staged approach later. Before I do so, I would like to outline the principal features common to all four parts of the Bill.
Initially, the Bill provides that each affected railway company shall forthwith resume operations of its railway and subsidiary services. Every employee shall forthwith resume his or her duties when so required. Each affected union and officers or representatives of these unions shall forthwith give notice to their members to facilitate the required resumption of railway operations and of employment duties. No railway company or any of its officers or representatives shall impede
Maintenance of Railway Operations
an employee from resuming employment duties when required, or in any way discipline any employee for having been on strike prior to the coming into force of the Bill. These provisions are designed to fulfil the main purpose of the Bill, that is, to restore the railway service operations that are of key importance to our economy.
Beyond the resumption of rail operations, the Bill provides for the extension of each relevant collective agreement and for the settlement of the collective bargaining disputes by arbitration. Initially, each collective agreement is extended for a two-year period ending on December 31, 1988, with provision for this term to be extended at the discretion of the arbitrator for a period of up to one additional year.
I have just mentioned the term "arbitrator". Hon. Members will note that the Bill provides that I should appoint such a person following the coming into force of the Bill or its various parts. The arbitrator will be required to decide all matters referred within 60 days, with discretion vested in the Minister of Labour to extend this period if necessary. The report of the arbitrator shall be prepared in a form that will enable its incorporation into the appropriate collective agreements. The agreements as amended will be deemed to have effect on and after January 1, 1987.
Arbitration as a final dispute resolution method will be found in previous Acts which Parliament has adopted to terminate work stoppages in the railway industry. The present Bill requires the arbitrator to determine all matters that remain in dispute at the time of that person's appointment.
I am aware that there have been suggestions from the opposition that the resolution of at least one of these issues should be predetermined by the House. Frankly, I believe that such an approach would represent an abuse of this House. Parliament is not a labour court and the House of Commons is not an arbitration panel. The conciliation commissioner's reports made it quite clear that there are several interrelated issues in dispute, the resolution of which would involve tradeoffs. These issues cannot be severed or dealt with in isolation from each other. Any Member who believes that they can does not in my view understand these labour disputes or, indeed, the labour relations process.

It would, of course, be preferable, Madam Speaker, to make the collective agreements part of a negotiated settlement. However, the parties have shown they were incapable of reaching an agreement through the bargaining process. The decision-making powers the parties could have exercised in pursuing the requisite compromise to reach a settlement will now be handed over to a third party.
I would nevertheless urge the parties not to completely abdicate their responsibilities. It would be in their best interests to put forward a number of sound arguments to support their positions before the arbitrator I shall appoint and to co-operate fully with this person.

August 27, 1987
Maintenance of Railway Operations
This would be the best way for the parties to obtain an arbitration decision that would fully consider their respective needs and aspirations as they affect the issues on which a settlement has yet to be reached.
I mentioned earlier that the four parts of this Bill refer to four disputes in the railway industry. Once this Bill is passed, only the first part, which concerns the dispute between the conference of Associated Railway Unions and the two main railway transportation companies, comes into force. This is the only dispute where there is a strike at this time.
The other parts of the Bill, Madam Speaker, will not come into effect until after their proclamation.
At this time it would be unthinkable to remove, from the parties to the other three disputes, the prospect of freely negotiating their own settlements. However, it would be equally unthinkable for the House to ignore the potential for further disruption to the nation's rail services which these disputes present. The economic damage which the present strike is inflicting would also arise and, in fact, it would be magnified by its cumulative effect, if railway operations were to cease as a result of further work stoppages.
Consequently, the Bill provides for the future termination of any work stoppages that may arise, and for settlement of the three other collective bargaining disputes in the same manner as will be applied more immediately to the dispute involving the Associated Railway Unions.
I take no particular pleasure in introducing back-to-work legislation. However, I have a duty to protect the public interest when it is threatened by the inability of private parties to settle peacefully their labour disputes. The present strike is inflicting considerable damage on the people and the economy of Canada. The damage increases each day the strike lasts.
1 am sure that Hon. Members are receiving representations from those whose vital interests are being compromised by the current shut-down of rail services. They are demanding that the Government take decisive action to restore railway operations. The Bill that is now before us orders such a resumption of rail services.
It should come as no surprise to the parties that this Bill has been introduced. They have had sufficient time and assistance to settle their own differences. They have failed to do so. If they had any doubt as to the Government's resolve not to endure a damaging work stoppage, it should have been dispelled by the telegram that I sent to them on Monday.
The parties have proved to be unable to respond to that urgent call for common sense to prevail in a final attempt at mediation. As a general policy, the Government does not believe in interference in the collective bargaining process. However, the parties to labour disputes should be left under no
illusion as to our determination to intervene when the public interest so dictates.
When the facts are clear that the parties have abdicated their responsibilities to resolve their own differences, and a grave threat to the national interest ensues, the Government will act with all appropriate dispatch.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, speaking on behalf of the Official Opposition in this House, I would like to say first of all that we intend to co-operate with the Minister, so that the Bill can be adopted as soon as possible and a strike that is paralyzing the Canadian economy can be stopped, also as soon as possible, and we can thus put an end to this economic bloodletting.
Second, 1 want to say that I sympathize with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux), who today has to table a Bill to pick up the pieces left by his colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie). 1 noticed the Minister of Transport was in the House during the Minister of Labour's initial remarks. He is the one who should have been tabling this Bill and who should have put in place the mechanisms required to protect both the Canadian railway companies and railway employees. What we are seeing today is the result of action that was ill-prepared and ill-conceived and basically a threat to the future of Canada's railway industry. I am referring of course to the transport industry deregulation which the Conservative Government and the Minister of Transport imposed on us without any guarantee or any safeguard for several sectors of our economy, and particularly without any protection for the workers in that industry. Quite clearly, this strike was to be expected.

It was absolutely no surprise; indeed, there was plenty of advance notice and warning. Because the strike came with plenty of advance warning, we on this side of the House, the Official Opposition, say that it could have been averted. It did not have to happen.
1 was listening to the Minister of Labour explain and describe the consequence of a strike. The Minister knew in advance that a strike was coming that would hurt and affect the economy. Indeed, he has received a number of representations which indicated to him that the strike was imminent, and that the strike should not be tolerated. 1 have a series of telegrams and letters sent to the Minister asking him to intervene, and intervene quickly.
I wish to quote a telegram sent to the Minister:
Regarding the rail strike. 1. Strike started this morning will be devastating to economy of Canada, especially western. 2. Obvious the parties cannot settle the differences between them. 3. The Government of Canada must intervene now and settle dispute. No point in waiting.
August 27, 1987

We know that there have been a number of Canadian companies that have indicated to the Government their displeasure at the manner in which the negotiation was going on. These companies knew that the inevitable was to come; it was a fix. The railways have almost been squeezed out of business by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and his insistence in going ahead with deregulation. The two railways had no alternative but to try to save some money on the heads of the workers. They knew that by being tough and unreasonable with the workers, they would get the Government, which first of all made a big blow to the railway industry, to come forward and try to save them with back-to-work legislation. There were no negotiations. There was no good faith at all in the process.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
While we were discussing Bills C-18 and C-19 the Minister was absent. I am glad the Minister is here to listen to what we have to say, because we have repeated time after time that deregulation will be devastating to the railway industry, and the Minister did nothing about it. Today we are faced with a terrible strike.
I wish to cite what Dow Chemical had to say. They sent two letters to the Minister of Labour, and I am sure he has had a chance to read these letters:
The Western Canada Division of Dow Chemical Canada Inc. at Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta is a major exporter-1.5 billion pounds per year of chemicals. We are also a major supplier to Canada's pulp and paper industry which itself is a major exporter.
Western Canadian exporters have always had a tough time selling Canadian products abroad facing competitions from countries with ready access to ocean transportation lanes.
One ace that Canadian exporters have had was their reliability factor-our Government is stable and transportation interruption has been minimal.
Can we afford to lose this Ace?
Our customers for Canadian goods abroad are facing the same economic realities that Canadian industry faces, and that means they must have their orders on time. Our division will lose $300,000 every day this strike continues and several times that in sales, but when you look over a list of Canadian exporters, Canada stands to lose much more in terms of future sales.
This is but one company explaining quite clearly its problems and difficulties when there is a railway strike.
All of this, I am repeating, Madam Speaker, could have been avoided if the Minister of Transport had been a little more sensible. All that the Government would have been required to do was listen to the unions, which came one after the other when we were looking at Bill C-18. The Transport Committee of this Parliament travelled across Canada and
Maintenance of Railway Operations
heard witnesses in every city it visited. One after the other told us that if the Government went ahead with Bill C-18 it would be devastating for Canadian railways. They gave examples of regulations in the United States and what happened after the Staggers Act was implemented there, which had tremendous consequences for the workers.
[ Translation]
Of course the Government could have heeded these remarks since we were told quite clearly that deregulation of the transport industry would throw a lot of people out of a job. The workers told us that on the heels of deregulation in the United States American workers had been displaced, far from their families in many cases, just so they could hang on to their jobs, but that a great many of them ended up on the unemployment rolls.

But it was not surprising that the Conservative Government did not want to listen to union leaders. We know that it does not very often listen to workers. Conservatives prefer to listen to big companies. They gave billions of dollars to the oil industry. They gave away I do not know how much money through tax concessions to some big Canadian families.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Conservatives gave away almost the whole of our generic drug manufacturing industry to please the multinational drug industries of the United States and Europe. Now we have the consequence of their actions to please big Canadian shippers. On the backs of workers, the Conservatives have imposed deregulation in the transportation industry to please some big Canadian shippers. We knew the Government was not going to listen to the workers, but at least it could have listened to CN and CP. Certainly the Minister of Transport could have listened to his own Crown corporations whose representatives appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport. They indicated quite clearly that the plan to deregulate our vital transportation industry would put thousands of workers in the railway industries out of jobs. They told the Government not to go ahead with its plan to give American railways the chance literally to grab billions of dollars worth of business in the Canadian market without at least ensuring that Canadian railways had the same access to the American market. The railways told us, the Minister of Transport and the Conservative Members on the Transport Committee, that jobs would be lost if Bill C-18 proceeded. CN and CP told us that they would have no choice but to reduce the labour component of their costs if they were to survive American competition.

Again, the Minister of Transport refused to listen. He turned a deaf ear to the two railway companies and the railway employees who appeared before our Committee. Interestingly, an American expert, an impartial observer, appeared before the Transport Committee and told us a few

August 27, 1987
Maintenance of Railway Operations
things that should at least have attracted the Minister's attention and made him more aware of the risk involved for Canada's railway companies. Let me quote what Mr. Dempsey, President of the Association of American Railways, came and told us at a sitting of the Standing Committee on Transport:

We do not have anything in the United States comparable, as you know, to your proposed competitive line rates. It might be, or it might not be, and I pass no value judgment on it, a good thing to have a rail system in the United States which is like the interstate highway system. It might be a good thing to have railroads compete with one another like supermarkets do. All that I can say about it without passing a value judgment is that it will wreck the system in the United States, it would just wreck it, that is all.
That is quite clear, Madam Speaker. The Minister of Transport with the advice of some officials, some-
[ Translation]
-theoreticians who were never exposed to the practice and realities of trade and competition, some officials who dreamt up a way to settle the problems of the railways and, sitting behind their desks, tried to convince people that Canada's railway system had to be completely overhauled.

Therefore, this Government stupidly bought Mr. Thompson's advice and created a terrible mishmash in the railway transportation industry. There is no experience of the comfortable line rate brought forward by the Government in any other country of the world. This is fiction, an imaginative thing of Mr. Thompson's that has been bought by the Minister of Transport and is now being implemented in Canada.
The President of the Association of American Railways said that if such a thing were implemented in the United States it would wreck the system. 1 am telling you, Madam Speaker, it will wreck the system in Canada, which we are now witnessing with this strike. It is a direct consequence of the irresponsible decision of the Minister of Transport to disorganize railway transportation in Canada. 1 blame the companies for being unable to convince the Minister to change the plans, but above all, I blame the Government for insisting on deregulation in the railway industry. Nobody-I say nobody-except the big shippers have asked for it. Everybody else who testified before the Transport Committee said, one after the other, that the plan was crazy. Today, because of the lack of action and lack of responsibility on the part of the Government, there is a strike.
1 would like to read from an article that appeared in the Toronto Star last week. It reads in part:
R. E. Lawless, President of Canadian National, warned recently that reduced rail services and lay-offs are "permanent and irreversible." But he also advocated compassionate treatment of employees who are the victims of deregulation. "There is no question" he said, "that we have to manage these changes properly and we have to treat affected employees generously."
But when the House of commons approved the transport deregulation package in June after a debate that attracted little national attention, the government ducked the problem of potential layoffs. Indeed, the Tories flatly rejected proposals by Liberal transport critic Andre Ouellet to give the victims of deregulation certain "last-resort" financial benefits available to other workers under the Labour Adjustment Benefits Act.
Surely it isn't too late for Ottawa to recognize the plight of railway workers who stand to lose their jobs due to deregulation and to reconsider some sort of safety net for them.

1 am not quoting this article for my own personal satisfaction. 1 am quoting it to point out that today's crisis, this railway strike, did not come out of the blue. It was predictable. In fact, we saw this coming last June, when we asked the Government to take action to prevent a strike. 1 quoted this article that appeared in the Toronto Star to put the present strike into proper perspective.
We Liberals say to the Government that the strike became unavoidable when the Conservative Government refused to include a safety net for the workers in its deregulation Bill. Since the beginning of this dispute, we in the Liberal Party have been telling the Government that if negotiations were to fail, any back-to-work legislation would have to contain provisions guaranteeing a certain degree of job security for workers in the railway industry.

I asked a question of the Minister of Labour, indeed pressed him to make sure that, if he cannot undo the wrongs of the Minister of Transport, then at least to be fair to the workers in this legislation. He is the Minister of Labour and it is his responsibility to take the side of workers.
I am surprised that I do not see some protection for the employees in the legislation. One good example of greater job security, which Liberal Members are sure would have been acceptable to the labour unions and which would not have imposed an unbearable strain on the railways, is the recent settlement covering about 1,200 workers at the Ontario Northland Railway.
There is a new clause in the collective agreement between the Ontario Northland Railway and its employees. Clause 7(a), which gives the employees a sense of belonging to an organization. If there are difficulties, they will not be treated as if they are dispensable. They will not be laid off without proper care being taken for them.

speechtext:
That is right. My colleagues remind me that most railway workers have been devoted employees and have worked their entire lives for the CN or the CP. They deserve better than to be kicked out of their jobs because the Minister of Transport decided to deregulate the railway industry.
This new Clause 7(a) indicates that any employee with seven years' seniority, as a guarantee of employment, as long as the workers agree, could take another job with the railway.
August 27, 1987

In some cases, it might be difficult to find another job for the employee, but then the collective agreement says that, should no work be found, the employee is placed in a waiting status until such time as a vacancy occurs within his or her classification. During that period, the employee's unemployment insurance benefits or his or her outside earnings will be supplemented to a level equal to 80 per cent of his or her weekly base pay until such time as a job is found.

It is obvious that the Government has a responsibility, bringing pressure to bear as it did on Canada's railway companies by forcing them to accept deregulation. It simply cannot wash its hands off this situation. I find this all the more deplorable that there is nothing in this piece of legislation comparable to what the Liberal administration did in 1973, the last time a similar law was adopted to force the rail workers back to work. The then Liberal Government had shown enough decency, generosity, sense of fair play and understanding of the legitimate concerns of these employees to give specific directives to the arbitrator so he would pay particular attention to the unions' claims concerning job security. 1 will quote Subsection 16(3) of the 1973 legislation. Subsection (3) of Section 16 of that act reads as follows:
(3) An arbitrator appointed under subsection (1),
(a)	shall closely examine the job security demands of the unions and fully explore the feasibility of a job security plan based on the principle of attrition;
(b)	shall not alter or amend any existing work rules or practices in a manner that could have an adverse effect on rates of pay, earnings or employment opportunities, or safety;
(c)	shall, for the purpose of the arbitration, have all the powers conferred on a conciliation board under section 175 of the Canada Labour Code; and
(d)	shall in respect of wages specifically provide for the adjustment of wages to any increase or increases in the cost of living where the arbitrator is satisfied that such adjustment has not been previously or adequately provided.
It stands to reason that, when a Bill stipulates that all the collective agreement clauses which have not been ratified by both parties will be submitted to the arbitrator, that the decision of the arbitrator will be mandatory and binding on both parties, and that the Government fails to give any instructions to the arbitrator, the employees can indeed expect the worst. As it is now the Government washes its hands off the whole thing and says: The country has been thrown into economic chaos because the railways have stopped all operations and the Canadian economy is losing millions of dollars as a result of this rail strike. Well, we will take the hard approach. We will pass legislation and force the employees back to work. As to their wages, working conditions and job security, let the arbitrator do whatever he may feel like doing.
Well, I say this is not the way to proceed. In a similar situation in 1973, the Government at the time at least had the good sense to give certain instructions to the negotiator or arbitrator appointed at the time, to protect employee interests.
Maintenance of Railway Operations
I want to outline very briefly the fundamental differences between the 1973 legislation introduced by the then Liberal Government and that introduced today by the Conservative Government. In 1973 we, like the Conservatives, decided we could not allow a railway strike to go on any longer because of the consequences for the Canadian economy. Therefore, despite our best wishes and hopes we introduced in Parliament back to work legislation. Let us not kid ourselves. It is always better to have a negotiated settlement, but we imposed a settlement in 1973 because we felt we had to do so for the sake of the Canadian economy. I do not quarrel with the Government in this case and we will co-operate in passing this legislation because we think the economy of our country cannot be damaged by a railway strike.
However, when we deal with the legislation on a clause-byclause basis, I will have a number of questions to ask of the Minister. Indeed, I intend to introduce some amendments which could, to a certain degree, ease the fear and anxiety of the workers that such legislation is inappropriate. I hope the Minister in his wisdom will be able to give guarantees to the workers and hopefully accept some of our amendments which could certainly appease the workers under the circumstances.
In 1973 we put right into the Act a provision stating that some money was to be given to the workers immediately. Effective January 1 of the following year they would receive 34 cents per hour. In that way the workers, forced by legislation to go back to work, were not going back empty-handed. They had not won the collective agreement but at least they had won something. There was some incentive to go back to work and do good work. In this legislation there is nothing like that.
While I am not sure the Minister of Transport understands anything, I am sure the Minister of Labour realizes that when these workers are forced back to work they could slow down the process. There are many ways to do that. Their productivity could decrease. It is not in the interests of either the railways or the employees to see a situation like that develop. I would have thought, in a spirit of good faith, the Government would put at least some money on the line to induce the workers to accept the legislation and go back and do their jobs effectively as they are accustomed to doing. They may go reluctantly. They will be forced by law and they are law-abiding, but if they have no incentive at all, they might go back reluctantly.
Second, the 1973 legislation contained specific instructions for the appointed arbitrator. These included directions to come up with a feasible job security program. He was to recommend a fair wage increase. The present legislation contains no such directions.
Third, in 1973 no time limit was put on the arbitrator. We are dealing with a number of unions and different employers.

August 27, 1987
Maintenance of Railway Operations
This is a very complex issue. Yet this legislation puts a 60-day limit on the arbitrator to come forward with the package. I accept the fact that the Minister has the discretion to extend that time, but I am afraid a 60-day limit will force the arbitrator to look only superficially at the problems. Those problems include job security as well as other issues which had been raised in the negotiations so far. I do hope the Minister is in a position to say to us that he will not hesitate to use his discretion to extend that time limit if necessary.
The arbitrator will have an immense responsibility. I do not want to cast aspersions on the Minister. I know he has to decide on who is going to do conciliation work, but the list of people available is not the one he would like. However, 1 had been told that the appointment of Mr. Douglas C. Stanley as the conciliation commissioner was very surprising. Not that Mr. Stanley is not a good conciliator, but his experience with and knowledge of the railways is minimal.
Some very complex issues have to be looked at by the conciliator, and the feeling is that the conciliation report did not thoroughly and correctly address those issues. That might have been one of the reasons why there was no success between the parties; the commissioner left a number of issues unresolved or untouched. It was certainly not to the satisfaction of the employees. Therefore, I say to the Minister, whoever you appoint as arbitrator, you have to be sure it is a person with full knowledge of the industry, well known by the parties, and a reliable expert in this area.
As we know, very few things have been agreed to at the bargaining table. The arbitrator is literally going to write the entire collective agreement. Therefore, he has to be someone who knows the railway industry very well.
As well, in 1973 the Liberal Government guaranteed no wage reductions. That might sound funny. People say, well, surely the arbitrator is not going to order a wage reduction. I do not know. 1 do not think it is appropriate that this legislation does not have such a clause. Frankly, if the two parties cannot agree on a wage package, it is too bad, but I do not think one party should suffer more than the other. Therefore, the real minimum is the status quo. I do not understand why the Minister of Labour has not included a clause precluding wage reductions as we did in 1973. The employees already believe that-

-the dice were loaded, that the whole collective bargaining process was useless because the companies did not want to negotiate a new collective agreement, since they had the assurance that the Government, in the first few days following the beginning of a rail strike, would inevitably introduce back-to-work legislation. Some clauses of the Bill tabled by the Minister contain phraseology that is very close to the terms used by the employers, which makes it very tempting to consider the possibility that the employers themselves drafted the Bill. I hope that is not the case. 1 not only hope that is not the case. I also hope that later on, the Minister will be able to
give me not just the assurance but irrefutable proof that he will give the arbitrator instructions that employee salaries are not to be reduced.
Finally, I may recall that in 1973, there was no provision for a financial penalty in case of non-compliance with the legislation. I wonder why today the Minister is imposing such severe penalties for non-compliance. We are now talking about penalties of $20,000 and even as much as $100,000 per day. In 1973, we in the Liberal Party placed far more trust in the railway employees' ability to observe the law, and that is why we did not include penalties. I think the Minister of Labour, who as such represents the workers, should at least show the same respect and the same trust. In concluding, I want to say that the Bill before the House today is a most regrettable one, but that should not surprise us because we have to pick up the pieces left by the Minister of Transport.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in speaking on this legislation I would like to state right from the outset that I am sorry that the negotiations broke down and no satisfactory settlement was reached. I think most Canadians feel the same way. We recognize that in such circumstances governments do have to act. However, the manner in which the Government dealt with this legislation and these negotiations proves its incompetence and shows why we must oppose this legislation. I will go into some detail later to explain exactly why 1 believe that to be the case.
However, let me start with what has happened in the House in the past week. We have been pushing the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) to act in a way which would help to resolve this dispute. We did not tell them to get into the negotiations themselves or to write every clause. We did, however, ask the Government to come forward with some policy on job security.
We explained the problems of people in the railway industry. We explained the obvious issue which was keeping the two sides apart. When we did that, the Minister of Transport got up and spoke about the present CN policy on job security and waxed eloquent, as he is wont to do from time to time, and did so passionately and wrongly, as he does quite often.
The present job security legislation has resulted in thousands upon thousands of people being laid off over the last number of years in our railway system.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
As a result of this legislation and of what has happened in this House this week, workers across the country feel that they are being picked on by this legislation. They knew that there would be back to work legislation if negotiations were not successful. They also knew that the negotiations were under the hammer of a Government in which the Minister of Transport had already spoken out in favour of the CN position. That in itself made the dispute very difficult to settle in a positive manner.
We will oppose this legislation. We will not prevent it from passing because of the numbers in the House of Commons, but we will debate it. We will point out in detail the problems with it. We will be moving the required amendments. I hope the Ministers responsible will be open to those amendments.
We want to give fair warning now that we know that there is no artificial rush to pass this legislation in the next couple of hours because we all know that the Senate is not even being called back to discuss this legislation until two o'clock tomorrow. Therefore, this House can in fact sit for some length of time and we can discuss amendments and ensure that we do not pass legislation in three or four hours only because there is a political desire among some back-benchers to do so.
It is apparent that government policy was the cause of the strike itself. It was the issue of job security which kept the dispute from being settled positively. That is the same issue that caused the labour dispute within Air Canada. That is the same issue that caused labour unrest at CBC, and the same issue that caused labour unrest at Canada Post. If the Government had a positive policy on job security for Crown corporations and other government employees, there could have been positive negotiation for its employees. However, that is not the case and the remarks of the Minister of Transport this week proved that to be the situation. Other governments have also dealt with technological change. They have dealt with economic setbacks. They have realized that people have not always been able to keep their current job.
It is important to realize that the workers at CN and CP were not asking to keep the same job until they retire. In fact, they were asking for employment security with CN and CP and that those corporations should do all that is possible to make that a reality. It is important to realize that.
It is also important to realize that in seeking this goal, those same corporations should not be contracting out work that was done by people who are now being laid off. If one has worked for CN or CP for the last 15 or 20 years and has been doing a
Maintenance of Railway Operations
certain job in a shop or in one of the running trades and suddenly it becomes CN policy, which is supported by the Government, that this work be shipped to someone or some corporation that has never worked in this area before, how can one feel that one's valuable work for the company year after year is being appreciated? How can one believe that this country's legislation or the collective agreement one has negotiated will provide protection?
Obviously, the lack of positive government policy on employment security and the fact that the Crown corporations negotiated in a vacuum has led to this labour dispute.
In addition, we know that deregulation has been cited not only by the employees as one of the reasons for the strike, but, despite what the Government has said, the employer has also indicated that deregulation is one of the reasons it will not act to provide employment security for its employees.

speechtext:
The Minister of Transport wants sources. He will get those later on in the day.
Let me turn to the Bill itself and compare it to what was put in place not only in 1973, and also deal with some of the problems this legislation is causing. Clause 4 of the Bill requires that the railways resume operations forthwith. It also requires that "every employee shall, when so required, forthwith resume the duties of that employee's employment." This means that the employer must start operations and the employee, whenever he or she is called back, must also begin working.
In 1973, that clause stipulating "when so required" was not in the back to work legislation. That significant change proposed by the Minister of Labour, presumably supported by the Minister of Transport, means that those companies can call back only those employees whom it wants to call back. In effect, it can have a lay-off taking place as a result of this legislation.
This legislation does not return us to the status quo before the strike. It gives a new power to CN and CP to pick and choose which employees it wants back. Certainly, it may have to follow the seniority provisions in the collective agreement, but obviously it is not required to bring back those employees it had working prior to the beginning of the breakdown in negotiations.
That is a major error and a change which the Minister of Labour has brought forward. We want to know why and we will be asking him when we get to clause by clause study.

August 27, 1987
Maintenance of Railway Operations
I will not mention some clauses right now, but that does not mean we support them. I only have 40 minutes for my comments and want to deal with some of the main problems we see with this legislation.
Clause 6(1) states:
The term of each collective agreement is extended to include the period
beginning on January 1, 1987 and ending on December 31, 1988 and may be
further extended by the arbitrator to include the period beginning on January
1, 1989 and ending on a day not later than December 31,1989.
That clause gives the arbitrator the sole right to extend that agreement from two years to three years. What is the reason for that provision? The only thing that both parties in the negotiations agreed to in October, 1986, when they began their negotiations, was that they wanted a two-year collective agreement. No one has said since then that they wanted anything different.
If this Bill was simply back to work legislation, it would not be giving this very innocuous and powerful authority to the arbitrator. It has nothing to do with the dispute at hand.
The danger with this particular power is twofold: first, it reduces the power of the employees to negotiate at a time when they felt they had the power to do so; second, it means that if the clauses of this agreement have not solved the problems that occur in the railway industry they may have to wait one entire year longer before they negotiate.
The other problem is that the positions of the company and the union do not relate to a three-year agreement. The monetary clauses were based on a two-year collective agreement. The conciliation report was based on a two-year collective agreement. Some of the clauses that have been settled already, in open and honest negotiations, were based on a two-year collective agreement. Why would the Minister of Labour introduce legislation which gives an arbitrator the power to extend that legislation for one year at his or her whim? That clause must be eliminated.
Let us turn to Clause 8. The arbitrator, whom we do not know and who may not have any experience in collective bargaining or in the transportation industry, especially with railways, is supposed to solve this dispute within 60 days, although the legislation provides the Minister with the authority to give the arbitrator more than 60 days. However, this is a very complex set of negotiations.
We are not dealing with one employer and one union, but with two employers and many unions, involving many different situations and many different present collective agreements. Sixty days will not be enough, unless the arbitrator restricts himself or herself to a very limited investigation and role in determining what should be in a collective agreement. In that case, an arbitrator obviously cannot write a comprehensive and adequate collective agreement.
1 am also concerned that the issues in dispute are not itemized in Clause 8. That was done in the 1973 legislation, and while it may not seem important to some people, because
the disputes may seem obvious, there was a press release by the companies today saying that there are three items in dispute. The union is saying there are seven items in dispute. Obviously, there is a difference in numbers, and that is something about which we should be concerned. The legislation, based on prior history, should spell out what should be dealt with by the arbitrator.
The Government, in putting this legislation together, rejected the advice that I, among others, gave in the House of Commons. We suggested that the Minister of Labour meet with both the unions and the corporations prior to introducing this legislation. We were not advocating any further delay because we knew this legislation would be dealt with prior to the end of this week. However, we believed that if the Minister of Labour sat down with the parties, he could have at least had the advantage of recommendations based on the 1973 legislation with respect to the items still in dispute. Perhaps this legislation would then deal with the issues that both sides feel are the issues. He did not do that. As a result, some of the things I indicated earlier are problems and concerns.
In addition, the Minister has not met with the people who are not on strike at the present time, those people who are laid off as a result of the present labour dispute. This legislation affects these people as well. It affects the people in the shop crafts council and the locomotive engineers. For some reason it does not affect the railway controllers. That is an interesting question. We would also like to ask later on why that particular group was left out of this legislation.
The problem is that even those groups, or some of those groups who are not on strike at the present time, are affected by this legislation, and at any time the Minister wishes he can proclaim those parts of the legislation which say those people are now covered by the legislation. That is what I considered to be negotiating with an axe to your head.
This legislation is flawed. If the two sides ever had the ability to get together to resolve the items in dispute at the present time, that is now not possible because they know they have this blanket legislation hanging over their heads. The Minister should have at least consulted with the people who are not now on strike and ensured by his actions, and by the actions of this Parliament, that we are not put in a situation where we actually destroy any ability of those parties to come together by themselves and resolve any potential labour dispute.
With respect to the people who are not on strike, the shop craft workers and the locomotive engineers, this legislation gives the arbitrator the power to impose a three-year collective agreement even though they might be sitting down trying to negotiate a two-year collective agreement. It gives the arbitrator the power to decide what items should be in the collective agreement and what items should not be. It gives the arbitrator the power to take a position which is less than the
August 27, 1987

company offered and make that the final settlement. Again, to repeat the words of my Liberal colleague, that can happen.
I know it can happen because when I was a teacher in northern Manitoba it happened to me. The school board offered a certain settlement. The teachers turned it down, not because of the monetary aspect with which they were quite happy, but there were other conditions they wanted included in a collective agreement. They made that case very clearly to the arbitrator. They said that money was not the issue. They were quite happy with what was offered. But they wanted other clauses put into the collective agreement. The arbitrator said no to each of the items the teachers wanted, and then decided to give us less money than the school board was willing to give us. Thank God we negotiated a settlement the next year and the school board gave us the money back. That is the irony of open-ended powers given to an arbitrator.
An arbitrator not only has the power to stay away from anything in the conciliation report, because there are no guidelines in this legislation, but he has the right to ignore what both the parties think might be appropriate. Surely an arbitrator should not be able to go beyond the bounds of where the two parties are at the present time. That just does not make sense.
We must admit then that in 1973 the Liberals, who had a minority Government, put together legislation which was perhaps a bit stronger than they would have put together otherwise, but at least the legislation in those days had a wage guideline. It had other guidelines. It told Emmet Hall, who became the arbitrator, to deal with the conciliation report. All of those things were done. That is not happening here.
The workers are also being penalized because this legislation does not give them any immediate guarantee of money. Not only do they get no guarantee of money in the long run, but it does not even give them the money the companies have promised them. Why is that? The conciliation report indicated that 3 per cent this year and 3 per cent next year, presumably with a two-year collective agreement, would be a reasonable settlement. The companies have offered about half that. Arbitration may take longer than 60 days. I believe that if we are going to order people back to work, we should also ensure that they receive at least some of the money in the short run instead of having to wait what may be well over 60 days. It may be over a year or two years. It is known that arbitration awards are not settled quickly.
Madam Speaker, this legislation is extremely flawed. I am certainly going to reject any attempts by government Members to rush this legislation through the House. I hope that in the long evening in front of us the Minister of Labour and his Department officials, who will be up watching this debate, and his other officials will get in touch with CN and CP and will talk with the unions, because if this House does not rush this legislation through there may be parts of this legislation which could be improved with the concurrence of all parties. Again, I used as just one example the strange powers which have been
Maintenance of Railway Operations
given to the arbitrator to extend the collective agreement by one year when no one has asked for it.
We should be able to have a list of what is in dispute so that the arbitrator knows what he or she should be dealing with. It may well be that in order to ensure some peace at the work site, the companies might be willing to give some monetary increase at the present time. All of that is possible if the Minister and his officials make the attempt to contact the people involved.
One of the problems we have when we rush legislation through this House is that we do not allow for those who are affected by the legislation to participate in the legislation and to make that legislation not only relevant but as complete and as accurate as possible. Therefore, I think the Minister has a long evening in front of him and I want him in the House as much as possible. I also want him out in his government lobby talking to the people who are affected by this legislation to ensure that we do get the amendments that are necessary, because the legislation can be improved. The way it stands right now, we cannot support it. We have indicated all week that we would wait to see what the package was. We did not want to be in a position of saying we were against back to work legislation if it was good legislation. We wanted to give the Government a chance to provide adequate legislation if negotiations did break down. But that is not what has happened. This is weak legislation. It is flawed and vague. It is the Minister's job to fix it. If he does not, then we will.

The Hon. Member for Papineau attempted to blame the present strike in the Canadian railway system on deregulation. How is it possible to blame this particular strike on deregulation when deregulation so-called, or the Canadian version of it, does not come into effect in Canada until January 1, 1988? Is this anticipatory? How can he possibly blame it on deregulation?

August 27, 1987
Maintenance of Railway Operations
Deregulation has not caused any loss of employment in the Canadian rail industry because we have not had deregulation. Of course, there has been a loss of employment in the rail industry in Canada caused by the changing nature of the transportation system. For example, in 1974 there were 107,569 employees in the Canadian rail system. In 1984, before we came into office, there were 81,710 employees working in the Canadian rail system, 25,859 fewer than in 1974. Is that to be blamed on deregulation when there was not even any deregulation at that particular time?
If we listen to the Hon. Member for Papineau, I suppose we should make it all retroactive-the blame is certainly retroactive. As a matter of fact, his Government was in office during all those years except for eight months. So the problem with the railway industry, and many other industries in Canada, particularly the smoke-stack industries, the heavy industries, is that the nature of our economy has changed. It has changed to a service and communications kind of economy. The smokestack heavy industries and the railways which depended heavily upon them have therefore suffered as a result. That is the problem that is faced by the railway industry.
The Hon. Member for Papineau suggested that when the committee was dealing with legislation passed earlier in this session leaders of the railway industry said that employment would be lost because of deregulation. 1 happen to have some of the quotations here, which is more than he did. He did not quote one. As usual, he made these slippery comments, old slippery-heels from Papineau, and he did not produce any quotations at all. I have here in my hand a quotation from Mr. 1. B. Scott, the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of CP Rail. He stated:
We would have to adjust our workforce-but that is going to happen anyway. Those cost pressures are there for our customers in the market competition aspect of rate-setting, let alone the regulatory aspect.
That was Mr. Scott's evidence when he appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport, as well as when he appeared before the Senate committee.
On July 14 Mr. Morin, the Vice-President, Marketing, of CN Rail, stated:
The total amount of traffic in volume may not be different on each of the railways, but it will move at a much lower revenue. If that is the case, then there will not be any job loss because of it.
This is exactly contrary to what the Hon. Member for Papineau has said everyone from the railways was saying.
Mr. Lawless, who is the President and Chief Executive Officer of CN Rail, said on March 2:
Whether this Bill comes in or not, the railways have to rationalize their services and they have to find a way to reduce their costs or they will not be able to remain competitive in the market-place today.
That is what he said. It is in direct contradiction to what the Hon. Member for Papineau said.
The rail industry faces a difficult, competitive situation, not because of deregulation but because of fundamental changes in
the economy. They faced it in the United States. They face it in every other industrialized country in the world. It is because of changes in railway technology, not because of regulatory reform.
Since the passage of the National Transportation Act in 1967, rail employment in both these railways dropped 29 per cent. In CN and CP freight operations, rail employment dropped 19 per cent in the five years from 1980 to 1985. So deregulation has no more connection with the present impasse in collective bargaining in the rail companies of Canada than the man in the moon would have.
If this strike were caused by deregulation, then what caused the strikes of 1966 and 1973? What a silly suggestion to make. This strike is caused by the fact that the two parties involved, management and employees, have not been able to reach an agreement on various aspects of their collective agreement. We have a free collective bargaining system in Canada. It has some penalties as well as a great number of benefits.
This industry is important to Canada. It is important to our grain farmers and our resource industries. What is carried by rail today, by the way, is grain, which accounts for one-sixth of all the railway tonnage, bulk freight, coal, sulphur, potash, steel, chemicals and forest products, which comprise over one-half of rail traffic. The smaller, more valuable traffic has gone to the trucks and all the rest of it. Because it is so important, we have to intervene. We cannot allow the rest of the country, innocent third parties, to be penalized in this way for very long. That is why we have to intervene.
Rail handles only 27 per cent of all freight tonnage today. That is still very important, which is why we are intervening. But in 1984 the rail system handled 33 per cent. So one can see the declining situation with respect to the share of rail in our freight transportation and the competition it faces from trucks, ships and air.
To return to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Papineau, I am intervening to set the record straight. He claimed that we should have known that the strike was coming and that we should have intervened earlier. We all knew that there was the possibility of a strike. We all know in any set of collective bargaining that there is a threat of a strike. There is always the threat of a strike. That is the power, the weapon, that the employees have, and the employer has the threat of a lock-out. We all know what can happen when negotiations are not successful. But because we know that, are we supposed to intervene right from the start? Is that what the Liberal Government did in 1973 or in 1966? Of course it did not. It is a piece of errant stupidity to suggest that somehow we should have intervened any earlier.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) did everything he could through the use of conciliation and the use of mediators to try to assist these two parties to reach a settlement. Because they have been unable to reach a settlement the House has to intervene to see that the disruption in the rail system of Canada ceases. The only way to do that is by the appointment

of an arbitrator. This House cannot and should not arbitrate this dispute. We are not capable of doing it. We are not impartial, as we all know. We just heard the opening speaker, the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy). He is obviously not an impartial observer of the scene. He has already given his opinion that work should not be contracted out and so on. We are not even allowed to give the facts with respect to the present collective agreement that is in effect at Canadian National.
When I was asked questions in the House on August 24 by the Hon. Member for Churchill, he objected to my answers and tried to allege that somehow this shows some type of bias. I was only explaining that the Crown corporation, for which we are responsible, has one of the more generous systems in effect in Canada, and that the matter was now subject to mediation and collective bargaining. We are not even supposed to say that our own Crown corporation has a system of job security at present. It is one of the matters that has been discussed in this collective bargaining negotiation, because naturally the railway employees want a better and a more generous one, and the employer has to be concerned about its costs, competitiveness, and productivity. They have a different point of view.
We are not even allowed to give the facts in the House when we are questioned and when the motives and the actions of our own Crown corporation are impugned. But the Hon. Member for Churchill can stand up and take a position on all of the matters that are disputed in the present situation, and give his opinion that they should not contract out work. What is sauce for the goose is not sauce for the gander. That is a typical NDP double standard. They think that they hold all the morality, and that all the rights are in the hands of the NDP. We all know how impartial they are. When the labour movement states that they are against free trade, the members of the NDP bob their heads and they are against free trade. If they are against deregulation, this crew bobs their heads and they are against deregulation.
I will say that the Hon. Member for Churchill put forward some relevant points on the Bill. They were of interest to hear. The Hon. Member for Papineau said that the railways have been squeezed out of existence by deregulation imposed by the Minister. How can they be squeezed out of existence by something that is not yet there? Deregulation does not start until January 1, 1988. How can the railways be squeezed out of existence in that manner? It is shocking. It is anticipatory squeezing. It is premature squeezology.
The Hon. Member for Papineau talked about labour adjustment. There are labour adjustment programs of Government. We are aware of the fact that the economy is changing and certain industries have to be assisted. There have to be adjustment programs. We have to deal with the problems of lay-offs and unemployment. My hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), was
Maintenance of Railway Operations
dealing with that, and it has been dealt with by the present Minister. Of course there are a number of government programs for employment and training. Companies like CN also have programs. I will not comment on whether or not they are adequate. I think it would be fair to say that they certainly have programs that are among the best in the Canadian industrial scene. I am speaking on this point to defend CN, which is our Crown corporation, from unfair criticism from the Hon. Member for Papineau-prejudice, criticism, political, polemical, putrid attacks from the poltroon from Papineau. That is why I am speaking.
The Hon. Member for Papineau criticized the fact that there is no extra money for the employees in the Bill now before the House. That is because this is a Bill to send this dispute to arbitration. How could we intervene and take one or two aspects of the present impasse in the relationship between these groups and deal with that ourselves in the House? We do not think that is the way that the collective bargaining system should operate. Despite our best efforts, these parties have been unable to resolve this matter themselves. It is not for the House to say what the collective bargaining agreement between them should be. Now they have failed themselves, it is for some other impartial authority.
I ask Hon. Members to remember that any new agreement that is reached or imposed by the arbitrator will be retroactive to January 1, 1987. The parties can still agree on any items that they want to agree upon when they first go before the arbitrator. If they say to the arbitrator that we agree on X, Y, Z, this item, that item, or 30 items, the arbitrator will not bother to deal with the items that they agree on. There is nothing stopping the parties from agreeing on anything at the present time right up to the arbitration. Under the legislation, the parties can agree after the arbitration. They can change the agreement that the arbitrator imposes, if the arbitrator has to impose an agreement, by agreement afterwards, as you will see by reference to the Bill. They can change the agreement. They can change their present agreement now, and they can change any agreement that the arbitrator finds he has to impose, if they agree together. Their fate is in their own hands, which is where it should be, if there is to be a free collective bargaining system, as this country is supposed to have. That is how this legislation leaves it. It leaves the dispute largely in the hands of the parties, but if they cannot resolve it then the appointed arbitrator will resolve it.

He did not say that the employers wrote the legislation, but he said it seems to some people, or it could be that-I forget the exact words he used-the employers wrote this legislation. The Hon.
