Minister. They have concluded that he does not take this rail strike seriously. He has used the opportunity to make jokes about a serious matter affecting some 55,000 or more employees rather than to justify this back to work legislation. He is making light of a strike that is costing the railway companies $20 million a day, a strike that is costing private industry tens of millions of dollars a day.
What we get from the Government is a Minister of Transport responsible for the railway industry making joke after joke. 1 would like to tell the Minister of Transport that members of the Official Opposition do not treat this matter lightly. We do not believe it is a joke that tens of thousands of Canadians are affected in a very negative fashion by this legislation.
Having said that, I would like to now turn to Bill C-85, a Bill entitled an Act to provide for the resumption and continuance of railway operations and for the settlement, et cetera, et cetera. It is back to work legislation. By its very nature, back to work legislation is objectionable. It is offensive in a country that believes very strongly in collective bargaining. However, there comes a time when the Government must act in the best interests not only of the unions and the management but of Canada as a whole.
We are faced here with a national emergency. Parliament was recalled several weeks ago to deal with a so-called national emergency on refugees in Canada. We questioned whether or not that was a true emergency or a true crisis, but the situation Canadians are faced with today is a true national emergency, a true national crisis. If Parliament were not sitting, there is no doubt that it would have been recalled to deal with this legislation as it has been on several other occasions.
The public interest commands that we pass legislation today to get the railways running. As of tomorrow, the railways will be running, notwithstanding members of the New Democratic Party.
1 would like to comment very briefly on the position taken by members of the New Democratic Party. We in the Official Opposition believe that their position is totally irresponsible. The New Democratic Party through its main speaker said that it intends to oppose the legislation unless certain changes are adopted. It was not quite made clear whether or not, even if all the suggested amendments were accepted by the Government, the New Democratic Party would in fact accept the legislation.
NDP Members would rather have the rail strike continue. They would rather have the railway companies losing $20 million a day. They would rather have grain farmers in western Canada suffer in a very serious fashion because of the rail strike. Members of the New Democratic Party would rather have the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are affected directly by the railway strike continue to suffer. Is that a responsible position for a national Party to take? I conclude that it is not. Members of the NDP are up to their mischief again. They are speaking out of both sides of their mouths.
August 27, 1987

Today I had the opportunity to speak to several representatives of the unions affected. Members of the New Democratic Party say they represent unions in Canada. Several union people had some difficulty getting through to members of the New Democratic Party to express their points of view.
If members of the NDP had taken the opportunity to speak to the unions, the individuals affected by this strike, they would have known that the unions themselves will accept back to work legislation. They have concerns about who the arbitrator might be and about some of the matters raised by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), but when push comes to shove, they understand that the railway must run.
Members of the NDP take the irresponsible and naive position that if some minor technical changes to this legislation are not accepted by the Government, they will oppose it. If there were an NPD Government in Canada, heaven forbid, then the railways would be closed, shut down forever and a day. There would not be a collective bargaining agreement entered into between labour and management.
As the Hon. Member for Papineau pointed out, we in the Official Opposition will support the Government. We are prepared to work all night long. As you know, the Senate has been recalled and it will be in a position tomorrow to give royal assent to this legislation which will be followed by resumption of railway operations.
The Hon. Member pointed out some of the deficiencies in this legislation, but we believe that, notwithstanding the deficiencies, the legislation is supportable. Unlike members of the NDP, who are opposed to everything, we will try in a very constructive manner to improve the legislation.
What are the changes we would like? We are concerned, as are the unions, about several matters. Let me begin with job security. Approximately 54,000 railway employees are affected by the strike. We are talking about 54,000 families. Is it too much for those people to want some type of job security? I suggest it is not. It is fine for us who sit in this beautiful Chamber and collect a pay cheque every month not to be concerned about job security, but the Government must be concerned about job security for the workers. We believe very strongly that certain guidelines should have been entrenched in this legislation to address the whole problem rather than simply giving the arbitrator a mandate to come up with some type of settlement.
In 1973, the Liberal Government was required to legislate railway workers back to work. That legislation contained specific instructions for the appointed arbitrator. Those instructions included directions to come up with a feasible job security program, avoid amending work rules in such a way that they would harm workers, and recommend fair wage increases. There are no such instructions in Bill C-85. In 1973, no time limit was set. Under Bill C-85, the arbitrator must do
Maintenance of Railway Operations
his or her job within 60 days unless the Minister in his discretion decides to extend that period of time. We believe that the arbitrator should not be required to do his or her important job while being worried about time constraints. Once again, we will attempt to convince the Minister to remove that clause.
In 1973, there was a guarantee of no wage reductions. There is no such guarantee in the present legislation. It should have been made absolutely clear in this legislation that there would be no wage reduction. At the very worst, the arbitrator should be allowed to maintain the status quo. There is a reason for that.
The workers are being forced back to work by law. There are provisions for fines in this legislation if they do not go back to work. It will be an offence for an individual to contravene this legislation with a minimum fine of $10,000 per day and a maximum of $50,000 per day if they were acting in the capacity of an officer or representative of the railway companies. A union official who breaches this legislation will be fined a minimum of $10,000 a day. There was no such provision in the 1973 legislation. The Government is holding a gun to the heads of union officials. That is not conducive to discussions in good faith. It is obvious that the Government, perhaps inadvertently, is tilting the legislation in favour of the employers. We will work with the Government to eliminate that provision.
Individual workers are also subject to substantial fines, a minimum of $500 and a maximum of $1,000 a day. That applies to individuals not acting in their capacity as representatives of the union. It seems to me the workers might not go back to work in a very positive mood. It also seems to me there are ways of ensuring they will go back to work and put in an honest day's work, as well as ensuring that they work with management and the arbitrator in order to come up with a report fair to all sides.
As you know, the workers can be legislated back to work or, to use the wording in the Act itself, be forced to resume their duties. However, we all know about working to rule. They may go back to work but they may not do anything that is not required of them. As you know, working to rule could be just as devastating and negative as a full-scale strike.
We believe that in order to show good faith certain provisions should exist in the legislation. First, there should be guidelines for the arbitrator with regard to job security, fair wages, et cetera. In our view that would assist to provide the atmosphere for positive, good faith discussions and bargaining. We believe that a time limit would assist in setting the right stage for a fair agreement. We believe that there should be no wage reduction.
We will try to convince the Government at least to legislate an increase as proposed by the conciliator. Rather than the employees having to wait the period of time required for the

August 27, 1987
Maintenance of Railway Operations
arbitrator to report, we believe that at the very least the workers should receive an increase in their pay cheques in the amount the conciliator has recommended. We believe that will show good faith by the Government.
I would like to comment very briefly on the cause of this crisis, this national emergency. In between jokes the Minister of Transport denied that this strike was caused by deregulation. He admitted, upon being pressed on the issue, that deregulation was a factor in this strike. We know that Bills C-18 and C-19, the two pieces of legislation which will deregulate the transport industry in Canada, have had a profound impact on this strike. The Minister of Transport should assume a lot of the responsibility for this strike because he dealt with this legislation in the same joking manner as he dealt with Bills C-18 and C-19.
As you know. Madam Speaker, there was a Cabinet shuffle today. I suspect that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), in his wisdom, will have recognized the lack of credibility of the Minister of Transport and shuffled him not only out of the position of Minister of Transport but right out of Cabinet. Given his propensity to joke about very serious matters, it seems to me that the Prime Minister and his Government would be well served by removing the Minister of Transport and replacing him with someone who will accept his or her responsibilities in a more serious way.
This strike was anticipated by a great number of individuals and organizations. During committee deliberations on Bills C-18 and C-19 the Government was warned that there would be massive lay-offs in the transportation industry.
I note, Madam Speaker, that you have indicated that my time is about to expire. Therefore, I will conclude my remarks by reiterating the position of the Official Opposition. Our position, unlike that of the New Democratic Party, is that we support this legislation. This is a national emergency and we will work over the course of the evening and the morning to try to convince the Government to adopt some, if not all, of the recommendations that we are proposing. We believe that by tomorrow evening this legislation will become law. I hope the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) will be able to convince his colleague, the Minister of Transport, to consider our amendments in a very positive way.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if there were laws in this country against intellectual pollution as there are against environmental pollution, the Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) would be one of the first to be prosecuted. He, better than anyone else, incarnates the current pathos of the Liberal Party, the well-deserved tragedy which is now coming upon that unlamented Canadian institution.
It would be funny, if it were not so offensive, to hear Liberal Members of Parliament making a case against deregulation in the course of this debate when we know that deregulation began under the Liberal Government prior to 1984 and that
many of the things which the Conservative Government has done would have been done by the Liberals had they survived the election of 1984.
We also know that during the course of debate in this Parliament about deregulation the Liberals played a very lacklustre part, both in the House of Commons and in the Senate. Quite unlike their behaviour with respect to Bill C-22 to amend the drug Patent Act, Liberal Senators moved no amendments and suggested no changes on deregulation. With respect, the Liberal position on deregulation, as it has been put in the House today with the concern that they have now developed about it, is probably one of the most hypocritical things I have witnessed here in a long time and, God knows, we have witnessed a lot of hypocritical things in the House of Commons. This ranks among the top 10, to be sure.
There are also funny things being said on the government side with regard to deregulation. We finally got the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) to admit that there is some connection between deregulation and this rail strike. Yet, after having admitted that, the Minister wanted us to believe that he never made any indefensible claim about deregulation.
I point to Hansard of August 25, 1987, where the Minister of Transport said, in reply to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), the following:
Mr. Speaker, this situation of the railways has no more to do with
deregulation than the hon. gentleman has to do with the moon.
That is not the sort of comment that Cabinet Ministers should be making in any event, but the Minister of Transport in effect withdrew that statement when he admitted to me this afternoon that deregulation is a factor. It is a factor because the last year of the contract which was being negotiated, 1988, is a year in which deregulation would already be in effect.
As I read into the record before, the conciliator himself, Mr. Stanley, notes on page 6 of his report that the railways see deregulation and relatively low wages as giving trucking an edge in this competition.
We are talking about the railways' attempt in this negotiation to anticipate the effects of deregulation. One of the effects of deregulation is that they will have to compete with the lower wages paid in the trucking sector. That means that railway workers will be asked, by virtue of government policy, to accept lower wages than they have traditionally been paid in order that the railways might fit into the deregulated framework that is being imposed upon the Canadian transportation sector by the Government. Lower wages for working families mean a reduced quality of life and reduced opportunities. It is not an exaggeration to say that deregulation was one of the biggest pieces of anti-labour legislation ever passed in the United States. We will come to see that deregulation in Canada will prove to be one of the biggest pieces of anti-labour legislation ever passed. We see the beginnings of that in this very dispute, in the way the railways have tried to anticipate the framework within which they will have to live after deregulation.
August 27, 1987

I do not say this to exonerate the railways because I think there are ways in which they can respond to the difficulties of deregulation without taking it out on their employees. For instance, they could have been more persuasive with the Government in making it realize the absolute lunacy of the policies that are being adopted as a result of deregulation.
Doctor Stanley says on page 6 of his report, again referring to deregulation, that all this leads to the railways' efforts to improve productivity to meet the competition from trucking and from the U.S. rail industry.
One factor, which is not unoriginated but comes right from the conciliator's report, is that one of the most ridiculous, unjust, unpatriotic unCanadian, and damaging steps the Government is taking is that of competitive line rates. Like no other country in the world, we will allow foreign-owned railways, in this case American railways, to compete directly for Canadian traffic that would normally be transported across Canada. Currently, traffic that might originate in British Columbia or Alberta would be transported across western Canada to points in eastern Canada or the northeastern United States. I find it incomprehensible that the Conservatives are making it possible this traffic which formerly made its way across Canada might cross the border from Alberta into Montana and be transported across the northern United States to points east.
This would eliminate the jobs of all the people who operate the trains, who maintain the trains, as well as the jobs of people in spin-off industries that the railway creates.
That is the Progressive Conservative regional development strategy for western Canada. It is eliminating all those jobs as a direct result of deregulation and Bill C-18. That is why the Government must take responsibility for creating the context in which this dispute has occurred.
Railway workers are not only arguing in favour of their own economic well-being when seeking job security and job protection from the effects of deregulation. They are on the front lines in the battle for the very transportation infrastructure of Canada. They are on the front lines fighting for the very nature of this country, if you like.
I hope we can finally put to rest any remaining contention that deregulation is not somehow involved in the present situation, whether it be negotiations, a strike, or back to work legislation.
1 have some concerns about the Bill itself. First, it is quite unlike the Bill that returned people to work in 1973. This is partly because the Bill in 1973 was passed by a completely different Parliament in which the New Democratic Party held the balance of power. We were able to have a much larger say in the kind of back to work legislation that would be passed at that time than we obviously will be able to have with the current Government. However, we have not given up hope that
Maintenance of Railway Operations
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) will listen to some of our suggestions.
Furthermore, this Bill is quite different in detail and in tone, which is especially disturbing. The tone of this legislation and the remarks that have been made, not by the Minister but by certain other government Members in the last few days, have shown that there is a prejudgment on the part of the Government about who is making the most legitimate claims in this dispute. Yet it is my opinion from the conciliator's report that he is more severe with the companies than the employees.
Some of the details of the Bill, which again related to its tone, were mentioned by the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy). For instance, workers are to go back to their jobs when so required. What is the meaning of "when so required"? Is it when the company decides it wants them back, or could they decide not to require some people to come back and require others? I hope this wording is only a sign of sloppy drafting rather than deliberately inserting into the legislation a new power for the railways to play havoc with the lives of their employees.
The Bill in its present form provides no guarantee that everyone who went out on strike, believing it was his or her right under the usual circumstances, will even be called back.
However, this afternoon there was a call for return to work, but under quite different circumstances than what 1 am describing. Some local yokel at the CPR diesel shop at Winnipeg decided, to recall the employees at that shop. The employees at the CPR diesel shop who belong to the Canadian Council of Shopcraft Unions are not technically on strike. They were to report to work immediately and therefore be put into the position of having to cross the picket lines of their fellow workers. This created a potential for a very ugly scene but, thanks to the intervention of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), who made a few phone calls to people in authority at Canadian Pacific, wisdom prevailed and the decision of the local yokel at the CPR diesel shop at Weston was overruled.
Why can the Minister not agree to the suggestion by the Hon. Member for Churchill that there be an itemization of those matters in dispute placed in the Bill? Why leave open the possibility that during the course of the arbitration the items in dispute will not be those things now being negotiated? Why not ensure that what is in dispute will be the subject of arbitration, rather than creating chaos upon chaos? The Minister should follow the suggestion of the Hon. Member for Churchill that those matters which are in dispute be itemized so that there is no disagreement about what is in dispute.
In his telegram to the railways on Monday ordering the parties to have one last round of negotiations the Minister cited the conciliator's report as the context in which they should be conducting their negotiations. Yet this legislation sets no context in which to proceed. There is no mention of the conciliator's report or any other guidelines or instructions.

August 27, 1987
Maintenance of Railway Operations
I hope the Minister will explain why he left out any reference to the useful context that this report might have provided to the arbitrator in the process that the Minister is setting up. Why did he decide not to have any guidelines whatsoever, or any minimum conditions for that matter?
It has already been pointed out that, unlike the Bill that was passed in 1973, there is no guarantee that there will not be any reduction in wages. There is no guarantee of anything. Workers who are going back to work are being asked to sign a blank cheque and put all their faith in some person who has been given no particular instructions or guidelines and all authority in a piece of legislation in which there are no protections whatsoever. There is no protection against rulings by arbitrators, which may be completely out of line with any sense of justice or what is happening with the railways. So I hope the Minister will take that to heart and consider amendments in that direction.
There are some things that one just cannot understand unless one is close to the issues. What has happened in the railway industry is that there has been a complete breakdown of trust over the last five years to 10 years between labour and management. For many people in the community I come from, in Transcona, the railway they worked for and knew for decades, the railway their parents and their grandparents worked for, as is the case with me, has disappeared. What we have now is a completely different world in which management, for whatever reason-and they will be stimulated to be even more like this as a result of deregulation-is constantly looking for ways to get rid of jobs, to get rid of people.
We see this also in the way in which rules are being enforced. Employees are constantly in a position where they are damned if they keep the rules, because if one kept all the rules set down for operating a railway there is not a boxcar that would move. They are damned if they keep the rules. In fact some of them have actually been subject to harassment by the company for keeping the rules. But by God, if they break one of those rules and an accident occurs, they have to take the rap.
At one time it was understood that employees were in a difficult position with respect to these kinds of things as well as with respect to other situations, but this acknowledgment has completely broken down, and so nowthere is no trust.
Let us take an issue the conciliator addresses but does not understand, that is, the desire of the railways to have trainmen hook up hoses. These hoses comprise the break system on a train. The railways say all they want is some flexibility. When there is no carman available whose job traditionally is to hook up these hoses, they want trainmen to be able to hook them up so they do not have to go halfway across the yard to get a carman to hook up the hoses. They say all they want is flexibility. However, anyone who works for CN now knows full well that that is not the real reason. The real reason the
railways want to get permission for trainmen to be able to hook up hoses is that they want to be able to lay off about 50 carmen. That is why they want that flexibility. So there is a built-in dishonesty in the bargaining.
There is a built-in lack of trust because time and time again things which have been asked for on one basis are known to be motivated by something completely different. The houses are a good example. With all due respect to the conciliator, he missed that altogether. For whatever reason, he just did not know the full story behind that request.
Railway workers cannot be expected to continue to work cheerfully or productively if they know that at every turn the company is looking for a way to get rid of them, and if they know that at every turn, in terms of public policy established by this Government, their own federal Government is looking for ways to provide opportunities for American railways to take their jobs away. That is not exactly the kind of thing that provides people with a sense of security, well-being or confidence that there is anyone on the government side who cares about them at all.
There has been some argument about whether we knew the strike was coming. We all knew the strike was coming. We knew it was coming because we knew we had a Government that was unwilling to instruct its Crown corporation, Canadian National Railway, to abandon the kind of concession bargaining in which it was engaged. Because we know that railway workers are human beings, that they have some dignity, that they do not intend to live on their knees, and that there was no way in God's heaven they were going to accept such ridiculous demands, we all knew there was going to be a strike. As long as there were self-respecting railway workers around, there would be a strike. It is on the Government's head, not on the heads of the railway workers, that this strike occurred in the first place. If the Government had two brain cells to rub together, it could have figured out what was going to happen, but it did not. So all the people who are complaining about the effect of the strike on their businesses or whatever, can look at the Government opposite and not anywhere else for someone to blame.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was interested in the comments of the Hon. Member with respect to the impact of deregulation as a cause, or one of the causes, for the existing strike at the present time. He stated in fact that deregulation, which will be going into effect on January, 1988, is really the cause of the current strike.
I wonder if the Hon. Member could explain to us why it was that between 1974 and 1984, when there was no deregulation in the country and when the present Government, of course, was not in office, there was a reduction in the total workforce of the railways of some 25,000 people, something like a 29 per cent reduction?

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would be delighted to tell the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) because there
August 27, 1987

has been an implication here-and the Minister of Transport was basically following the same line-that somehow because there were significant reductions in the railway workforce prior to deregulation, therefore, any argument we make about how deregulation will reduce the numbers even further is somehow illegitimate. That is a complete non sequitur, as far as I am concerned.
Yes, there were significant reductions in the railway workforce prior to 1984 and it did not have anything to do with the deregulation. Big deal. So what? What bearing does that have on my argument that deregulation as such will make an already bad situation worse? The already bad situation we are in with respect to the reductions in the railway workforce has happened because of some factors over which no one had any control. I am quite willing to admit that. The use of hopper cars as against the traditional wooden boxcar, the reduction in the traffic of bulk commodities, the change in the economy from a less resource-based economy to a more service based economy, all had a bearing. However, just because there were legitimate factors involved does not mean we should be silent about the voluntary things that were done.
The things I just mentioned were involuntary. They were things no one could do anything about. But there are things that have caused the rail workforce to be reduced that people could have done something about, things which were a matter of public policy. For instance, the present Government refused to instruct the railways to abandon their policy of renting rolling stock by the thousands from the United States railways which put people out of work in Transcona, Moncton, Point St. Charles and right across this country. The Hon. Member has probably seen those yellow rail boxes on trains. The next time he is stopped by a train, he should count just how many rail boxes are on the train. Those are American cars. They are repaired in America, they are made in America and when it is all over they will go back to America, and every time the Hon. Member counts an American rail box, he can count Canadian jobs gone down the drain because this Government did not have the guts to tell the railways to make their own boxcars here in Canada and to use Canadian-made equipment.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we meet here today to deal with the suspension of the nation's vital rail operations which began on August 24, 1987, after many months of bargaining, conciliation and mediation. It is somewhat ironic that it is almost 14 years to the day since the last time the House was called upon to deal with a national rail strike.
I look around in the House and I see the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). I am sure that he remembers in 1973 as a new Member of Parliament the violence that went on during that rail strike. I am not naive enough to blame the Liberal Party for the violence that went on. The Liberal Party was in power but it in no way had anything to do with the violence. I blame the unions for the
Maintenance of Railway Operations
violence at that time. However, I do blame the Liberal Party of the day for the way it handled the strike. It took the Party 14 days before it started to deal with the problem. The Government of today is in charge. It knows that after eight days we are entering a critical period, when economic effects will be felt by the people of the country. People become very restless. We have moved on this, and we have moved substantially. We will settle the situation.
The last 14 years-indeed the last 20 years-have seen vast technological change, innovation and subsequent worker adjustment on the railways. The new competitive environment stemming from national and international forces requires that labour and management seek better ways to adjust to the changed economic circumstances. As has been emphasized by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux), this disruption of services has the potential to cause widespread economic loss in national and international trade, to an extent that would endanger the welfare of our nation.
The significance of rail transportation to Canada is reflected in the fact that about one-third of the total freight tonnage in Canada is moved by the rail mode. Many bulk commodities, of course, can only be moved economically by rail. Many manufacturing industries and our resource sector depend heavily upon the rail industry.
Rail passenger traffic continues to play an important role in Canada's passenger transport industry. It, too, is significantly affected. It is the interruption of this vital social and economic communications link that is the subject of my comments today.
Vital services on VIA Rail, GO Transit and the Montreal area commuter system have been disrupted by the withdrawal of operating crews and facilities provided by Canadian National and Canadian Pacific, the major companies involved in the present dispute. It is reported that about 30,000 Toronto area workers who use GO Transit daily and about 25,000 Montreal area commuters will have to seek alternate transport to and from their places of employment.
Let us think about the impact this will have. Tonight, later on, I will be flying to my riding of Mississauga. I have to drive into Toronto later on tonight. I am told that Queen Elizabeth Highway and Highway 401 are completely blocked, bumper-to-bumper. The people of this area are not going to sit at home. They are industrious people who want to get out and go to work, and they are going to work, but at great inconvenience.
The traffic congestion and general disruption to normal work schedules and associated travel can only have negative economic and social consequences for the many individuals and businesses dependent on these services. While alternate travel arrangements are being put in place for the commuters affected, the alternatives have reached the limits of their capacities. The situation in Montreal and Toronto is well beyond being a mere inconvenience. It must be resolved, and it will be resolved.

August 27, 1987
Maintenance of Railway Operations
It was only last year that VIA Rail celebrated the one-hundred-and-fiftieth anniversary of rail passenger service in Canada. VIA Rail, which employs some 6,000 workers in all regions of Canada, and operates 800 trains per week, carried 6,286,000 passengers last year. VIA Rail was established 10 years ago following a government decision to reorganize the rail passenger system and to create a single entity to deliver service to all Canadians.
In that 10-year period thousands of employees were transferred from Canadian National and Canadian Pacific and integrated into VIA operations. Station and maintenance facilities were acquired, while the new company endeavoured to modernize in an effort to retain existing rail travellers and to expand in the highly competitive passenger travel market. It is noteworthy that the transfer of workers from Canadian National and Canadian Pacific was accomplished with a high degree of co-operation between the railway companies and the many unions involved. Unfortunately, these co-operative efforts have been disrupted due to a work stoppage on our major railways.
The Government continues to be dedicated to the important goal of making VIA Rail an effective and efficient transportation system for all Canadians. It is crucial that the current railway strike not jeopardize VIA Rail's future potential in this respect. Canadians must not lose confidence in VIA Rail's ability to provide reliable, uninterrupted service across the country. The historic unifying role of the rail passenger system in Canada must be retained for the benefit of all regions.
1 would like to mention a few words about GO Transit. GO Transit carries daily 61,000 passengers to and from work, about 30,000 people. It has been my pleasure many times to meet with these people in GO train stations in Meadowvale, Streetsville, Erindale, Cooksville, Dixie, and others in the riding which I have the honour to represent. The GO trains also travel through Oakville, Clarkson and Port Credit. I know that these people are being very seriously affected. I know that they want to have their mode of transportation returned to them, and we plan to do that.
VIA Rail is making an effort, with the support of many train users and train lovers, to expand its role in the Canadian tourist and general travel industry. It is attempting to tailor and upgrade services for those thousands of Canadians who either prefer to use the train or who, for economic or other reasons, have no other viable alternatives. To many Canadians the passenger train is a vital link that has major significance for their personal lives.
In the interest of maintaining VIA Rail's contribution to this country's rail transportation system, I support Bill C-85, the Maintenance of Railway Operations Act, 1987. This back to work legislation is responding to a serious situation in which the railways and the nine unions involved in the Associated Railway Unions coalition have made every effort, with extensive third-party assistance, to resolve their differences. But they have not succeeded. We believe that moving in five
days is the way to go, and I know Canadians support us in that respect.
After the many collective agreements involved terminated on December 31, 1986, the parties engaged in direct negotiations among themselves in an effort to resolve their conflicting demands. As a result of requests under the Canada Labour Code, Part V, to the Minister of Labour for conciliation assistance, a conciliation officer was assigned. The officer's efforts were also unsuccessful.
Subsequently, an outside expert was appointed as a conciliation commissioner to aid the parties in settling the many contentious outstanding issues. When the report of the conciliation commissioner did not succeed in providing the basis for settlement, the Minister of Labour named a mediator to try to bring labour and management together. These efforts, too, ended in an impasse.
On August 24 the Minister of Labour directed his Associate Deputy Minister, Bill Kelly, to meet with the parties in a last-ditch effort to arrange a negotiated settlement. The union workers and railway management know that this Government has done everything possible to reach a settlement. All of these extraordinary efforts have been to no avail.
I listened with interest to the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) discuss the railway worker reductions over the past number of years. A few moments ago, the Hon. That should make it obvious to the most ignorant Member of Parliament that the railway workers of Canada and their unions are not Luddites. Mr. Speaker, we have known similar disputes in other vitally important sectors of the transportation industry that are subject to Division V of the Canada Labour Code. These disputes were also a threat to the national interest. At the time, various groups loudly demanded a major reform of our approach to the collective bargaining process, and invariably, some very well-intentioned people recommended taking away the right to strike or to declare lock-outs from the parties concerned. 1 say well-intentioned, Mr. Speaker, because these people are usually concerned about the impact of work stoppages on innocent third parties who have no say in settlement of disputes by which they are affected. They may be well-intentioned but I think they generally have a poor understanding of the complexity of labour disputes and the importance of the right to strike and to declare lock-outs as part of the labour relations practice that has developed over the years in Canada, the United States, Western Germany and other major industrialized democracies.
Division V of the Canada Labour Code provides measures to ensure that collective agreements are implemented and provides a comprehensive and flexible mechanism to facilitate the bargaining process.
Mr. Speaker, upon examining the provisions of the Code concerning the settlement of disputes, I was impressed by the flexibility these provisions offer for settling various problems in the collective bargaining field. We cannot expect a single policy or guideline to consistently resolve labour disputes. The flexibility provided under the provisions of the Canada Labour Code relating to the settlement of disputes is truly admirable and reflects one of the most sensible approaches developed over the years in the labour relations field. I feel the Canada Labour Code offers all the flexibility we need in an effective mechanism for settling disputes.
The right to strike or declare lock-outs exists only seven days after the Minister has exhausted every avenue provided by the conciliation process under the Canada Labour Code. Furthermore, the Minister may, at any time, in accordance with Section 195 of the Canada Labour Code, appoint a mediator to assist the parties to a dispute in settling the dispute.
Under Section 171 of the Canada Labour Code, the parties may, at any time before the Conciliation Commissioner or Conciliation Board makes his or its report, agree in writing that the recommendations of the Commissioner or the Board shall be binding on the parties. Briefly, Mr. Speaker, this procedure offers management and the unions all the resources of the conciliation and mediation process, to assist them when negotiations become deadlocked and also leaves them free to make use voluntarily of a mechanism that will help bring

Mr. Speaker, the Government has tried to encourage private sector initiative in Canada to a far greater degree than before and to discourage resorting to government assistance to achieve economic and social ends. This attitude with respect to the role of the state gives individuals more responsibilities and, in the field of industrial relations, labour and management should feel some kind of obligation to settle their differences without government intervention.
As a matter of fact, this happens to be the purpose of the conciliation and mediation procedures provided under Part V of the Canada Labour Code: the first responsibility of the parties involved is to negotiate and resolve their conflicts. In certain cases they may need third-party assistance to shed light on complex negotiation proceedings. In this respect, conciliation and mediation procedures have been established to help labour and management achieve their ultimate aim, namely sign a collective agreement.
In that context the role of the state is to make things easier.
Although Canada Labour Code Part V sets the limits of the rights and responsibilities of the opposing parties, such limits obviously include responsibility for solving themselves the differences which come up during collective bargaining talks.
Mr. Speaker, these limits are prerequisite to what we sometimes refer to as free collective bargaining dynamism. In a way, the responsibility of the parties give them the driving force which enables them to seek common grounds, fair and reasonable compromises which reflect all available options, and to convey to their rank and file or to their senior management the outcome of the collective bargaining sessions.
The Labour Code strikes a balance between the rights and obligations of each party to the collective bargaining process. This framework paves the way for and promotes a renewed sentiment of mutual respect without which collective bargaining remains an idling mechanism.
Unfortunately, there are times when, for whatever reason, management and unions forget they have a responsibility to settle their dispute and try to shift that responsibility to a third party, usually the Government.

Thank you. 1 am still pleading.
The words "when so required" are really not necessary. Those working with the railroads when this strike began should be working with them when it ends. If there are to be any with lay-offs, then those lay-offs should be justified, and, not take place simply because the railroads were given the option by the Government in this legislation to not call back any more workers than it absolutely had to.
I ask the Government to consider that point because there is already too much unemployment with the railroads and with former CN family companies. These job losses most seriously affect the smaller communities which, in many cases, are one-industry communities. They include small communities in eastern Canada in my area of Nova Scotia and other Atlantic provinces, as well as farming areas of western provinces.
These jobs are important in those areas because they not only provide wages for the employee and his or her family, they provide an economic base for the respective communities in which these employees live. It is important to maintain these services in those communities. The downstream effect of deregulation will be a loss of service and a loss of jobs in many communities. The fact that they will no longer be able to offer railroad service will affect their opportunity to attract new industries.
Clause 6(1) of the Bill states:
The term of each collective agreement is extended to include the period
beginning on January 1, 1987 and ending on December 31, 1988 and may be
further extended by the arbitrator to include the period beginning on January
1, 1989 and ending on a day not later than December 31, 1989.
I object to that clause as well. It is not the Government's
role to bring a new aspect into the negotiations. I believe that
one of the key questions in negotiations would be the term of
August 27, 1987

the agreement. That is for both sides to agree upon and, presumably, negotiations have been going on in that regard. If the parties have not agreed on a term, that is an outstanding issue.
I suggest that it is beyond the scope of the Government's responsibility to ask Members of Parliament to allow the arbitrator to increase the term of this agreement from a two-year agreement to three years. That is beyond what the Government should be trying to achieve with this legislation, and I would ask it to delete that clause.
It is not its role to recommend points of negotiation to the sides in this dispute. It is not our role in Parliament to tell the arbitrator that he should be considering points that are not already being discussed between the parties in this dispute. It sets a very dangerous precedent for the Government to become involved in suggesting to the arbitrator that the term can be extended from two to three years. It represents the thin edge of the wedge, where the Government can then put anything into legislation that it believes the railways should have obtained but, in their knowledge of the situation, chose not to negotiate.
The Bill also includes stiff penalties for non-compliance, including lock-outs and strikes before December 31, 1988. These penalties are between $20,000 and $100,000 a day. There were no penalties in the 1973 legislation with which the former Liberal Government dealt. I believe it is better to leave that question to the arbitrator because there could be very good reasons why these penalties could be more or less than the ones suggested by the Government. It is not the Government's role to suggest the penalties.
I believe Clause 8 will have a great effect on the arrangement that will be achieved once the Bill is passed and the arbitrator has completed his or her task. Clause 8(1) states:
The Minister shall, after the coming into force of this Part, appoint an arbitrator and refer to the arbitrator all matters relating to the amendment or revision of each collective agreement that, at the time of the appointment, are in dispute between a railway company and a union and the further extension of the term of each collective agreement permitted by subsection 6(1).
Clause 8(2) states:
The arbitrator has, with such modifications as the circumstances require, all the powers and duties of an arbitrator under section 157 of the Canada Labour Code.
There are no guidelines provided for the arbitrator. There is nothing to compel the arbitrator not to reduce the benefits already held by the workers. There is nothing which would restrict the arbitrator from bringing new items into the negotiations.
I think it is important that the arbitrator has some guidelines, certainly as far as the workers are concerned. There are no legislated increases. In 1973 there were guidelines for the arbitrator. The 1973 legislation as well contained specific instructions for the arbitrator which included the direction to come up with a feasible job security program, not to amend
Maintenance of Railway Operations
any work rules that would harm workers and to recommend fair wage increases. I do not think it is asking too much to have those guidelines included in this legislation. As I say, we are trying to balance the rights of the workers against the rights and duties of the companies.
The companies already have a very strong advantage because they have had the knowledge that the Government was going to bring in back-to-work legislation, and they may have had some idea of what this back-to-work legislation was going to contain. I do not know that. I am not making any allegations, certainly, but it is a possibility. I do feel, however, that what the Government should be doing is helping the workers, trying to do something to safeguard the workers with respect to this legislation and the role of the arbitrator.
There were no time limits set on the arbitrator in 1973. This legislation sets a 60 day time limit which can be extended only at the Minister's discretion. While it is important and vital that the railways move again because the economies at the extreme ends of our country depend on the railroads, 1 do not feel we should be blinded in pursuing our goal of bringing the railways back into operation to the rights of workers. Too often that is done. I think we have only to look at the situation which has existed in our country over the last 10 years to see how railways have not only reduced their workforces but I think, to a large extent, reduced the relative position of the workers of the railway companies vis-a-vis other occupations in this country.
Workers for the railroads had every opportunity, for example, for a secure and valid pension plan, but too often railroads did not protect the older workers. For instance, a man who retired at age 65 with what he thought might be a satisfactory pension, found out at age 82 that the railroads had not added anything to his plan and that inflation had eaten away the benefits of that plan and he was really in one of the most unfortunate economic positions in the country. There are a great many workers today in that position. That is one aspect.
Another aspect is that quite often workers' benefits are given when it depends upon the urgency, political or otherwise, of the situation. I would like to mention as an example the situation of the Moncton shops.
I feel the workers of the Moncton shops were treated quite well. I would like to have seen them get jobs, but I thought the benefits that were offered were good benefits. However, a lot of people, particularly workers at CN in Atlantic Canada, although they thought the benefits were very good too, were upset because these benefits were not offered to them.
Take the case of a man who retires, for instance, at age 55. The workers at Moncton were able to take pre-retirement without any penalty at age 55. Other workers who were not working at the Moncton shops and were between age 55 and 60 had to accept a penalty for every year they were below the age of 60 when they retired. That was just because their layoffs in the downgrading of CN in their area did not receive as

Maintenance of Railway Operations
much attention as did those at the Moncton shops. I think that is unfortunate. 1 do not think that should be the case.
I think the treatment should be standard across the country, particularly in small towns where the job is at least as important as it would be in any other area. That person's job should be kept in mind and that person should receive the same treatment as a worker in a larger centre. I hope the Government will take this into consideration and try to do something.
The Government stated in the Budget that it is concerned about the older workers who are unemployed. 1 think fair treatment with respect to pre-retirement would do an awful lot to help these older workers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been asked today to consider Bill C-85 which orders the resumption of work by Canada's railways and provides for a mechanism to determine the final terms of settlement between the parties. It is perhaps obvious, but nevertheless important to point out, that this Bill would not have been necessary had the parties to the railway disputes been capable of meeting their responsibilities under the Canada Labour Code, Part V, by renewing their own collective agreements.
Despite considerable conciliation assistance provided to them by the Government, they were unable to do so without a work stoppage. This work stoppage, principally involving a strike declared by the Associated Railway Unions at midnight on Sunday, August 23, has paralyzed railway transportation and has brought key sectors of the Canadian economy into jeopardy. The Government cannot, and will not, tolerate a shut down of the nation's major transportation system. I am certain I share the sentiments of all Members in recognizing the critical importance to our national economy of the passage of this timely legislation.
As we consider this legislation, we will want to bear in mind that the present dispute is having immediate effects on various sectors of the economy and that decisive action by this House tonight is required under the current circumstances. I want to emphasize to the House, and draw out the particulars of the impact of this railway dispute on the western economy. Indeed, as we consider the legislation before us, we all want to bear in mind its immediate relevance to the grain farmers in the prairie provinces and in other provinces, including Ontario and Quebec.
The Province of Ontario and the Province of Quebec each have within their boundaries substantial acreage of grain production of various types, whether it be wheat, rye, flaxseed or corn. The grain economy in each of these provinces is affected by this railway dispute. In the western economy, the grain producing areas located in the prairie provinces are our richest endowment of domestically produced grain for domestic consumption and for export. The importance of the legislation before us in dealing with the devastating impact threatened by this present rail dispute certainly cannot be over emphasized.
I cannot stress enough the importance of this dispute to small businesses and to the small towns throughout the prairies which rely on the railways to transport grain, potash and other basic commodities that are the income base to the prairies and provide the source of livelihood for thousands of our citizens.
When we think of the western economy, and the vital importance to it of the grain economy, what comes to mind will most likely be the major grain terminal operations at Thunder Bay and the Lakehead and on the West Coast, Vancouver and Prince Rupert. This is as it should be, because it is at these points that the activities of approximately 2,000 primary elevators throughout the Prairies, as well as the trucking and railway transportation industries, are focused.
Thunder Bay and the West Coast ports are the focal points of the industries, as well as the major points at which grain is processed for shipment by water to our export markets, either directly from the West Coast or indirectly from the Lakehead to the numerous elevators. Most of our eastern-bound export grain is stored temporarily in transfer elevators at Montreal, Quebec City, Port-Cartier, and other eastern locations, awaiting shipment to our European markets.
It is this complex infrastructure of grain production and transportation that is affected by the railway dispute, a dispute between private parties which has brought to a halt the movement from the Prairies of more than 7,000 railcars of grain per week and which threatens a devastating blow to the western economy.
I want to make clear to Hon. Members my reasons for supporting this Bill and what I see as its necessity. The conditions under which prairie grain farmers compete in the international grain markets today reflect developments that have unfolded over a number of years. These are developments that have been clearly adverse to the pricing of internationally-traded grain and, consequently, to the dollar return to the farmers and the western economy of each bushel of grain produced.
One of the most significant developments in this regard is the increasing ability of some of Canada's international grain competitors to grow more grain. This has contributed to a growing world surplus and has led to further developments that have had some severe effects on our grain producers. I am referring here to the effect of the world grain surplus on grain prices and to the attempts by major market competitors, especially the United States and the European Economic Community, to expand their share of the world market by the use of export subsidies that have amounted to billions of dollars. The efforts of these countries to export their grain have been nothing short of formidable.
The decline in world prices has made it all the more important that Canada export a larger volume of grain to compensate as much as possible for the weakness in international grain prices. In this regard the crop year ending July 31,
August 27, 1987

1987 has been a year of success in that, according to the statistics of the Canadian Grain Commission, bulk exports of grain and oilseeds totalled a record high of 30.2 million tonnes, surpassing the previous record attained in 1983-84 of 29.9 million tonnes, and last year's exports of 23.7 million tonnes.
Canada's railway companies and the workers on their networks and in their shops have made a vital contribution toward the attainment of yet another record for the western grain economy. Their achievements need to be recognized. In doing so we must also underscore the necessity to the western economy of uninterrupted rail transportation services. Elundreds of thousands of workers in resource industries, including forest products, coal, potash, grain, as well as the chemical and fertilizer segments of the western economy, face lay-offs as declining sales and a rippling effect throughout the economy are threatened by this rail strike.
We have not had a national rail transportation stoppage in approximately a decade and a half. The stability of collective bargaining negotiations has been a positive factor in our grain export achievements during that period of time.
As 1 mentioned, western grain farmers are already struggling to survive in an era of collapsing world prices and overproduction. They desperately need the income which comes from a steady sale of the grain they produce. These farmers are vulnerable as well to the loss of markets, the loss of sales, which could result from a prolonged strike.
You know, Mr. Speaker, there is no shortage of grain available in the world. The subsidy war between the U.S. and the European Economic Community already threatens to erode traditional Canadian markets. Any difficulty getting Canadian grain to export ports is an open invitation to Canadian grain customers to turn elsewhere. Canada is a country dependent upon its railways for commerce, and we need action now.
1 would now like to talk a little bit about coal in western Canada. In 1985 the coal industry produced a record 60.7 million tonnes, 45 per cent for the export market and 55 per cent for the domestic market. The coal industry has become a direct source of economic activity for several provinces. Elowever, 93 per cent of Canada's reserves of minable coal is located in western Canada, especially in British Columbia and Alberta, with some in southern Saskatchewan. Development of coal deposits depends on many factors, but transportation is the main one.
The Pacific Rim is Canada's largest market zone. In terms of individual countries Japan, South Korea, Brazil, France, Hong Kong and Taiwan are the top six. Western Canada moved 32 million tonnes of coal in the year 1985 to all regions, that is, both domestic and export markets. Our export customers depend upon Canadian coal for its quality, its reliability and its security of supply. We must move the coal.
Tourism is another major industry for Canada. Alberta depends upon its rail service to attract and transport tourists
Maintenance of Railway Operations
into its two well-known parks. Banff and Jasper are indeed unique mountain park resorts that depend upon tourists for their livelihood. Over four million people visited these recreational areas last year, many via train.
Forestry is a number one industry in the Province of British Columbia, and it is a growing industry in Alberta, especially northern Alberta. The mining industry in central British Columbia and Saskatchewan relies on rail transport, as do all resource industries.
As I said before, because of its size and its geography, Canada is a country which must have rail service. And it must have continued, dependable rail service.
The level of economic activity in the western economy, as in our national economy, is vitally linked to the operation of our railways, as is the necessity of the legislation before us this evening. It is legislation which we must review and debate. I ask all Hon. Members to support Bill C-85 and to give it speedy passage here and now. It is extremely important for all of Canada, especially for western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, normally I preface my remarks by stating that I am pleased to contribute to a debate on certain legislation. Sometimes I agree with the legislation, sometimes I disagree, and sometimes I wish to see improvements. I must say that tonight it is with very little pleasure that I am required to make comments on Bill C-85, the back-to-work legislation to end the strike, particularly because of the manner in which it is being done.
As a Member of Parliament from Kamloops, British Columbia, a city, and a region, through which both the CN and CP railways pass, and I recognize the value the rail systems plays in my constituency in terms of the employment that is created, and the infrastructure provided for economic development.
Tonight we are dealing with something extremely serious; I think we would all agree, an emergency situation. When the rail transportation system of Canada is paralyzed, a good portion of the economy quickly shudders to a stop. It is unfortunate that in the latter part of August the unions and the two railways involved reached an impasse, and a strike was the result.
Because of the importance of this labour dispute and the fact that it touches the lives of so many Canadians, either directly or indirectly, one might get the impression that labour strife or strikes, or back-to-work legislation in the railways is a common phenomenon which takes place on a regular basis. Such is not the case. We have been blessed with relatively few railway disputes and national strikes. By and large there has been complete labour peace.
For many years labour and management have been able to negotiate their differences at the bargaining table. In the last 35 years there have only been three national rail strikes in

August 27, 1987
Maintenance of Railway Operations
Canada. That is a compliment when one considers the size of the operations, the thousands of employees, and the large number of unions involved. It is a compliment to the process of free collective bargaining. It clearly indicates that on balance free collective bargaining functions well. In the last little while such has not been the case.
I think it is important that we identify what we are doing here tonight. The Bill before us needs considerable improvement before I, personally, would feel comfortable in seeing it through to completion. Naturally, we plan to propose many amendments tonight or tomorrow morning as the debate continues. We are committed to being here in our places tonight, in the morning, or during the day, whatever it takes to complete thorough discussions and examination of this Bill and put forward what we consider to be the appropriate amendments.
It is also fair to point out that if we feel it is necessary to debate this issue all night and into the morning, the Senate has not been recalled until two o'clock tomorrow afternoon at which time it will be in a position to begin its stage of debate on Bill C-85, so nothing can proceed beyond that time. We do have ample opportunity to discuss the ways and means of improving this Bill which requires workers to return to work.
I think it is also useful if we ask why this strike occurred. When one looks at the facts, it does not seem to have anything to do with the unions or the companies involved. If we wish to identify the cause of this strike, it has to be the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada and the Conservative Government. I wish to take a few moments to articulate why I believe that to be the case.
We all remember the hours and hours of debate on the transportation Bills that were commonly referred to as the deregulations Bills. The Government decided that it was time to deregulate the transportation sector, and particularly the railways. As those discussions continued it became clear to all people who were knowledgeable in this area that if the Government proceeded with the deregulation Bills the result would be massive lay-offs in the rail transportation industry. No one would dispute that fact. The evidence was clear, namely, the experience of the United States, where they have already gone through deregulation, and where tens of thousands of railway employees were tossed on the scrap heap. Countless witnesses explained that that would happen in Canada if the Government proceeded.
As a matter of fact, it was worse than that. The deregulation Bills introduced by the Government included provisions found nowhere in the entire world. These deregulation clauses are not found in any other jurisdiction. Experienced people came before us, and I remind Members that the president of a railway in the United States came up here and said that if this deregulation goes through it will actually wreck our rail systems. Those are very strong comments. In light of the evidence before us, the Government soldiered on with its
ideological commitment to deregulation. With the massive majority of the Government it was able to pass the legislation in the latter part of June.
As officials from CN and CP stated to each of us individually, and certainly collectively in the committees and in the various forums where we received information, this would result in a disaster for the railways, and that they would have to significantly cut back their labour force. The railways felt that on average they would lose $560 million a year. That amount would be knocked off their balance sheets. As the Canadian rail system was put in direct competition with the American rail system and trucking companies, the result would be massive lay-offs; the railways would be forced to cut deep and mean in order to maintain a competitive edge in the transportation market-place.
Who wanted deregulation? The railways and their employees certainly did not. The large shippers did. They got through to our friend and colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and some of his associates, and presumably used their corporate muscle and decided that in the best interests of the country, the rail system, and what has made this country, which is our rail system, that they were going to go ahead and wreak havoc on the critical transportation infrastructure of Canada.
Now that is all history. The Government went ahead, as it said it was committed to do, and it deregulated. The important thing that we should recognize today is that the employees of the railways are the victims of this legislation. Those hundreds and thousands of men and women across the country are no longer employed by our national rail system. The victims of deregulation were the men and women who worked for the rail companies.
I am sure that most Members of Parliament have railways going through their constituencies. We know the rail workers, and know that they are committed, dedicated employees. These people seem to be a lot more closely associated and committed to rail transportation. They have a proud feeling working in this critical transportation sector. Fathers and sons, and sons of sons have worked for the CN or CP. That is a compliment in terms of the commitment shown by these employees to their type of work. How have they been treated? The Minister of Transport with his deregulation said that they were prepared to write off thousands and thousands of railroad employees. They may be victims on the scrap heap, but that is the way it is. That was the view of the Minister of Transport.
One would expect a little more from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux). After all, presumably he is concerned about what happens to labour on our rail systems and elsewhere. One would have thought he would have taken some steps to provide a safety net, so that when thousands and thousands of people lost their jobs the Minister of Labour would have an obligation, a responsibility to ease the pain and do something about the situation.
August 27, 1987

Some people ask what can be done; what options does the Minister of Labour have? What can we do in collective agreements, not so much in preserving jobs. 1 think job security is a misnomer. It is really employment security that we are talking about. In other words, if you have worked with a rail company for many, many years and that part of your work is being contracted out or technological change makes it redundant, you do not just take that employee and say " So long, Joe" or, "So long, Mary, you are on the scrap heap, you are on your own. Thank you for 20 years", or five years service or whatever. 1 think it is time that we showed some sense of compassion, some concern, some interest and took steps to provide some safety mechanisms.
I want to hold up as an example-it is not a perfect one, but it far ahead of where the Minister of Labour is taking us with this legislation-the Ontario Northland Railway. In its agreement with its employees there is a clause, 7(a) which says that anyone with more than seven years' seniority with that railway has guaranteed employment. Ontario Northland does not guarantee that job forever. That would be silly, but it says that after seven years of good employee performance that person is guaranteed employment. If that job is phased out through technological change, the company moves the individual or retrains him for another job within the Ontario Northland Railway. If there is simply no job at that moment for that man or woman with seven years seniority, then that person is put on waiting status through a variety of mechanisms and is able to collect 80 per cent of his or her regular pay until a job comes up in the company. It is done successfully and it is negotiated into the collective agreement.
There is no reason that we cannot do something for our employees. By that I mean CN's employees, the government run railway, and also for those of CP. There is no reason that major corporate railways like that could not have that type of employment security built into the contracts, as opposed to the present treatment, which is to boot out the people, and that is it.

In 1973 when we legislated an end to that rail strike there was a real difference. It was a Liberal minority Government, and I suspect because of that there was a little more sensitivity to the agreement. A number of things are absent in this legislation that were there in 1973, and that is the crux of the matter that we are debating tonight.
We are asked as responsible elected representatives to sign a blank cheque tonight, to buy a pig in a poke. This legislation says that we want you, Member of Parliament, to support legislation that will identify an arbitrator. Will it be Bill Kerkhoff in B.C., Peter Pocklington, or in all fairness, will it be Bob White or Jack Munro? Who will be the arbitrator? It is a very critical situation. It is imperative, since the arbitrator has only 60 days to resolve the issue, that the individual knows
Maintenance of Railway Operations
the transportation industry inside and out. He or she should be an expert and an individual respected for fairness in judgment; honesty and equity in decision-making. That is important. However, there is no reference to that in this legislation.
What are the guidelines? What is this arbitrator going to do? There is no guideline, no direction, and there is no suggestion. There is no blueprint or strategy. It is just, do whatever you want, Mr. Arbitrator. That is what the law is going to be and that is what the workers and the companies will have to accept. That is silly, Mr. Speaker. Who in their right mind fulfilling a responsible position as a Member of Parliament would support something so open-ended?
For that reason I want to remind the Minister of Labour that back in 1973, when similar legislation was introduced, it had guidelines for the arbitrator clearly laid out, guidelines in terms of what the wage settlement ought to be as well as a whole other set of guidelines. It laid out what were the issues to be resolved. It said, follow the basic recommendations in the conciliator's report. Members of Parliament could at least make a reasoned decision whether or not to support it.
Now we are asked to sign a blank cheque and to have faith in the system or in some individual to impose a reasonable settlement. That is really asking a little bit too much as far as I can see. We are expecting a lot when we say that the arbitrator must resolve this matter within 60 days, although there is a provision where the Minister can extend that time somewhat. We are talking about two major employers, many, many unions and thousands and thousands of employees right across the country. With only 60 days, we will need someone with an incredible amount of knowledge who is able to do an incredible amount of investigation very quickly, and I think that is a bit unrealistic.
There is no reference in Clause 8 to what are the disputed items. The union says that it has identified seven major areas of dispute. That was in the media today. The companies say that they have identified only three areas of dispute. Obviously there is some difficulty as to what is the problem at this point. Again, the legislation should have that included and it should also include something about general wage settlement areas. I know when our amendments as they come forward will suggest a four per cent range. That is the cost of living. In the conciliator's report there was general agreement that something over 3 per cent would be more than reasonable. I do not think anyone would say that the cost of living increase of 4 per cent for the first year is unreasonable. To indicate our good faith as elected representatives we feel that is a reasonable guideline for the arbitrator to pursue. We could go on and on.
