speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to take part in the debate today on Bill C-85, particularly as a Member from British Columbia. The situation that we have been faced with over the past week has had a detrimental impact on British Columbia and if allowed to continue would have a devastating impact on our B.C.'s economy.
1 want to start by complimenting the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) and his cabinet colleagues for the very prompt, decisive and fair action they have taken to put an end to the railway strike in Canada. That is what the people want the Government to do, to act fairly, decisively and in a timely fashion. That is what they have done on this occasion.
As the Minister and some of my colleagues have said, no one
wants to intervene in a labour dispute. One would hope that
the regular negotiation process would be successful and that
parties to a dispute could find the answers themselves. Obviously, in some cases, as in this case, that has not been possible, despite the best efforts of all parties, so it is essential that the Government intervene and bring in this legislation today, and hopefully by Saturday morning the railways can be running and the freight moving across the country.
We know that 30 per cent of Canada's freight is carried by rail and has therefore been affected by this work stoppage. However, I want to point out the particular importance of rail in British Columbia. In British Columbia, 90 per cent of freight is carried by rail. Considering that fact, one recognizes how important it is that we get the railways back to work.
When thinking of British Columbia, one thinks of resources. Coal comes from eastern British Columbia to the ports and overseas. Potash comes from the Prairies to British Columbia ports by rail. Grain, which is just now coming to harvest, moves by rail to the West Coast and on to foreign ports. All this is totally reliant upon prompt and efficient rail movement.
Of course, lumber is not as totally dependent on the railways, but certainly for some parts of the pulp and paper industry rail is an essential component which enables those commodities to get to market. We talk about essential services. I cannot think of a service more essential to British Columbia's industries than rail transportation.
Over the last few days, I have read some of the commentaries in the Vancouver press and I would like to share these with some of my colleagues so they can recognize the concerns and feelings that exist in British Columbia.
The Vancouver Province ran an editorial two days ago headlined: "A long rail strike can't be allowed". The Vancouver Sun ran this headline: "Coal, timber, grain halt as freight strike starts". Again, The Province had these headlines: "Strike raises anger", and "Shutdown hurts B.C.". Yesterday, the headline read: "All eyes on Ottawa", because it was recognized that the representatives of the people of Canada and of British Columbia would now have to take action.
1 do not necessarily always agree with the editorial policies of my local newspapers, but I would like to share a few comments from a particular editorial with my colleagues as I think it does enunciate well the importance of what we are doing here tonight. It reads as follows:
The Mulroney government really can't wait very long before legislating an end to the national rail strike. This is essentially a strike against the nation and it can't be tolerated more than a few days.
Either the negotiators must find a voluntary settlement early this week or the government must bring in a back-to-work bill and have the dispute settled by arbitration.
A coast-to-coast transportation system may not be an essential service in the sense that life and limb are threatened. But a rail shutdown is different from any other-
-if it goes for long without its railway freight system, the national economy will, to a large extent, grind to a halt. The damage from a rail shutdown would affect too many industries, too many communities and too many people for us to allow it to go beyond this week-
The dispute should be sent to an independent arbitrator or arbitration board.
August 27, 1987

So the story goes. 1 think that enunciates very well the feeling that it is so important to bring an end to this strike through government intervention.
Indeed, on Monday of this week the Premier of British Columbia called for a legislated end to the labour strike. He indicated that he would be talking to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and he said the following:
-I will tell him that the country can't afford this strike, not when key
industries like wheat, potash, coal and forestry are affected. This is the only
means for transporting these products, and I would go so far as to say strikes
shouldn't be allowed in the rail sector to begin with-
Let us look at another aspect of the strike. Perhaps it is not as essential, but hundreds of British Columbia travellers are steaming mad because their plans have been derailed by a Canada-wide railway strike. That is a human aspect of the strike of which we are all aware.
There have been indications that a walkout of more than a week would cripple British Columbia because the provincial economy relies heavily on port traffic. I refer to both export and import traffic. The Vancouver ports will become stalled because much of the containerized traffic moves from the ships right onto the rail.
Indeed, we know of the excellent record of the Minister of Labour when earlier this year it was necessary to legislate the longshoremen in British Columbia back to work. What came about as a result of Mr. Weiler's findings was the elimination of the container clause, and that has certainly been a very important benefit to British Columbia. We appreciate that kind of support.
In the nearly four days since the strike began, these are the facts of life. In British Columbia, Westar Mining Limited is facing $10,000-a-day demurrage fees if the railways do not start operating today because it has ships that are due in at Westshore Terminals; it will not have the products to put on them and it will have to pay the penalty because it has already ordered the ships and it is too late to send them back. The Saskatchewan Potash Marketing Agency notified customers that it can no longer guarantee shipments. At least one producer in the province says that it may have to close. The Coal Association of Canada has said that the strike threatens Canada's international reputation as a reliable supplier of coal and petrochemicals. The Alberta Wheat Pool said that Ottawa should get the railways moving first and then deal with the labour issue. The Dow Chemical plant in Port Saskatchewan, Alberta, could lose $300,000 a day and will have to shut if the strike is prolonged. Ipsco of Regina will be forced to cut back steel production and lay off employees if rail services are disrupted for just a few days. CGTX Inc. of Red Deer, Alberta, a company that repairs railway tank cars, has issued layoff notices to 43 workers and may have to close in two weeks.
It is not only the 48,000 men and women who are directly involved in rail work who are affected, it is all the other men and women in the other industries who are beginning to be
Maintenance of Railway Operations
affected. Certainly all Hon. Members on all sides of the House agree that we cannot let a strike in the rail services continue. It must be brought to an end.
One of the other issues I feel is very important is reliability of service. Canada and British Columbia are dependent on exports, and our customers expect their products when they are promised. If we cannot deliver, there are a lot of alternative bargains to which they can turn.
We need only look at the example of what happened in Australia over the past few years as it developed a reputation of having strikes and being unreliable in delivering products. That has certainly had a tremendously adverse impact on Australia. We cannot afford to let that happen. We must keep those products, the wheat, the potash, the coal and the lumber, going through those ports. That is another very important aspect of the issue.
What has happened in the process leading up to the legislation we are dealing with today? It has been difficult but I compliment the Minister. I think he made a tremendous effort to achieve a negotiated settlement. In his remarks earlier he indicated that he approved a full range of third party assistance which is available under Part V of the Canada Labour Code, hollowing direct negotiations between the parties he appointed a conciliation officer in an attempt to assist both the railways and the unions in the resolution of their differences. When that approach was unsuccessful a conciliation commissioner was assigned to the dispute to provide additional assistance in an effort to achieve a mutually satisfactory settlement. When his report was provided to the parties there was a request for mediation assistance and Mr. Carson was appointed by the Minister. Despite his efforts, major differences remained and that blocked the achievement of a new collective agreement.
As a further indication of the commitment of this Government to the collective bargaining process, earlier this week the Minister appointed the Associate Deputy Minister of Labour, Bill Kelly, along with Mr. Carson, to make a final attempt to assist the parties in reaching an accord. We have seen it on television every night. They have been meeting around the clock. Certainly we know Mr. Kelly's tremendous reputation for obtaining settlements in these disputes, but with all his skills and expertise it was still not possible to reach a negotiated settlement. Thus the Minister gave notice to the House that we would have to bring in the legislation we are dealing with today.
There has been some concern expressed from the other side of the House that 60 days is not an adequate time for an arbitrator to come to a settlement. It certainly seems to me that within 60 days an arbitrator would receive the full range of views and should, indeed must, come to a settlement because both the railways and the unions are going to have to know where they stand. I think you need that sort of gun to the

August 27, 1987
Maintenance of Railway Operations
back to get things going and get it over with, and I fully support it. Indeed, it is very appropriate that in this legislation the Minister has seen fit to include provisions to deal not only with this particular work stoppage but any other stoppage resulting from the negotiations presently going on between the railways and other unions. We will not have to come back and deal with a different Bill each time.
I also believe it would be very foolish to put conditions on the arbitrator in the sense of telling him what he should be doing. It seems to me an arbitrator has to look at all the facts and proposals and come forward with the best combination. His or her hands should not be tied by this legislation.
I have really been quite amazed by the position of the NDP in this matter. They told us this evening they cannot support the Bill. Yet earlier this evening an NDP Member said that they know the Bill will go through and just because they are opposing it will not mean the railway workers will not go back to work. What hypocrisy. What does that tell the people of Canada? The NDP claim that they could form the next Government of this country. If they did, what would their position be in this situation? Would they order the railway workers back to work or would they let the strike go on with the resulting devastation to the economy? They cannot talk out of both sides of their mouth. The Canadian public will not take it. They are not that stupid. This is only one example of the NDP trying to fool the public and we are going to see many others. I hope they come to their senses and support this Bill and ensure that the railway workers get back to work.
1 know there are others who wish to comment on this Bill and we want to get it into Committee of the Whole as quickly as possible. Therefore I will conclude by repeating that there are, unfortunately, situations where collective bargaining fails and the Government, as the defender of the public interest and caretaker of the economy, must intervene and prevent irreparable harm to Canada. This is one of those situations. We all regret the necessity for parliamentary intervention in the collective bargaining process, but on this occasion, and I believe all my colleagues will share this view, we must do it. This in no way detracts from the resolve which I feel must be exhibited to deal with situations in the future, but in this situation we must move quickly to ensure that the Canadian economy proceeds on course and is not crippled.
I therefore urge all Members to give this legislation their full consideration and support, and promptly pass it so that the Senate can deal with it tomorrow. In that way the railways will get back to work and our goods will once again be moving across this country from Newfoundland to British Columbia and into our ports on Saturday morning.

I will repeat that for the understanding of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie). The Canadian people are not so stupid as not to understand the position of the NDP. It is unfortunate that the Hon. Member for Capilano does not share that same level of understanding. She has documented the obvious at great length. There is no question in the eyes of the NDP, nor, I think, in the eyes of any Member of this House, that a national railway strike constitutes a severe test, indeed a threat to our economy. There is no doubt that this country cannot bear a strike that would have such severe economic and human consequences as this strike would cause if it were prolonged. Let us dispense with the necessity for elaborating too much on the self-evident.
We are faced with a serious problem. However, when looking at the impact of this strike on the Canadian people and our economy it is necessary to do what the previous speaker failed to do, and that is look at the situation of those who have been driven to strike. I do not recall in my boyhood my father saying, "Oh, God, I am going to have to strike this week. 1 have been working too long, I want a couple of days off with no pay and no food". I do not remember anyone saying strikes were nice ways of bringing about settlements. I do not think most people on strike enjoy not answering the door when the bill collector calls. Let us make sure we understand that a strike is not an option easily chosen by those who strike. It is the ultimate weapon against economic power that ordinary workers must use as a means of ensuring that there will be seriousness at the collective bargaining table.
Let us also take note of a few additional facts, one being that the workers in the railway industry have looked around and, from time to time, noticed that one of their fellow workers is no longer working with them. Day by day fewer workers are employed in the railway industry. Others have pointed out the changes in transportation and our economy generally that have brought that about. However, the fact is that thousands have found themselves unprotected after years, indeed in many instances after decades of having worked faithfully for the railroads. When it is all over they find that they not do not have jobs, they have no hope of jobs.
I think that most of us who are not trying to make pretty television pictures for an audience in British Columbia understand that there are some severe human issues involved here. One of the most significant human issues, sometimes 1 think not seen in human terms, is the threat posed by deregulation. One would have to have a very short memory not to recall the consistent warning provided by this side of the House that mimicking the process of deregulation which has occurred in the United States would mean that thousands of workers
August 27, 1987

would lose their jobs in the transportation industry, most particularly in the railway industry.
There are a lot of factors operating in any case as 1 have previously enumerated. Superimposed upon that now is deregulation. Mr. Speaker, can you think of any rational human being or collectivity of rational human beings who would not try to protect themselves against a situation which is a threat to their very survival, their economic well-being and the well-being of entire families? Can they on the other side of the House not understand that that which is at issue here is fundamental to the lives of a great many people?
The New Democratic Party has said that it is opposed to this legislation. We believe that it is possible to take the human equation into account in an appropriate way, even when faced with the imperative of having to legislate back to work within the context of the overwhelming economic threat which it constitutes.
However, we will vote against this legislation because it is so typically Conservative. It is part of the pattern of this Government when facing a crisis to go to the most extreme measure, divorcing itself as much as possible from the human issues involved. If the Government truly shared, on the one hand, the concern about the need for urgent action and, on the other, the need for humane action, we would be able to sit down as three different political Parties and approach in a reasonable way the drafting of this legislation.
We have prepared amendments for presentation which would make the legislation at least acceptable. We know, of course, that the Government will reject them. We know that the Government will once more abuse its overwhelming majority and impose legislation that will fail to take into account all that should be taken into account in the circumstances. Therefore, we will oppose what surely will be voted on, that is, unamended legislation presented by the Government.
Perhaps the Hon. Member for Capilano does not understand what the New Democratic Party is saying, but I am sure there is sufficient intelligence out there in the real world to understand what 1 have just said and what the New Democratic Party is saying.
In referring to legislation passed in similar circumstances in 1973 we find guidelines for amendments that might be accepted; guidelines that would make this back-to-work legislation tolerable. The 1973 legislation provided minimum guidelines for wages. A direction to provide an award was given to the arbitrator. After so many months of negotiations and being faced with back to work legislation, the workers would have at least some financial improvement in their situation.
In fact, we have a conciliation report which recommends 3 per cent over each of two years. I do not understand why, if the Government wants a humane piece of legislation, it cannot accept an amendment which would do such a thing. I do not
Maintenance of Railway Operations
understand how the Canadian people could accept that; the Canadian people are not stupid, and they know what is reasonable and humane and what fails to take into account all sides, as the Government so consistently does.
There is another difference between this legislation and that of 1973. The legislation of 1973 returned the workers to work under the status quo. The legislation now before the House says that operations are supposed to resume forthwith, but with respect to workers going back to work it says that they will do so when so required. This could mean that any number of workers presently on strike may not be called back, in effect could be laid off. That is certainly not fair in a situation where the key issue is job security. We understand why that provision is there, because the Minister of Transport has already declared which side he is on with respect to job security.

What does he think caused the problem between 1974, when there were 107,000 employees in the rail industries in Canada, and 1984, when there were 81,000, a loss of 25,000 jobs? Deregulation was not even in the air in that 10-year period. What does he think caused the loss of those jobs?
Can he not have at least some intellectual honesty and admit that a lot of the problems in the rail industry today are caused by the change in the nature of our transportation system, not by some sinister plot of somebody who is going to deregulate and put people out of work, and all the rest of it. None of us want to see people out of work. You do not have a monopoly on virtue. You do not have a monopoly on the good feelings. You do not have a monopoly on helping people. I have been helping them for 20 years and I am not NDP, nor a Liberal, I am a Conservative. Why do you think you have all the compassion and sympathy? You are a bleeding heart. You are bleeding that stuff, but you have no more of it than I have. I want you to answer that pragmatic question. What happened in those 10 years?

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I had hoped that we would hear from another member of the Government on this very important matter. I guess my colleagues to the right of me are spending their time watching a past Leader on television rather than being concerned about the legislation that is before us.
I wish to do two things in my contribution to the debate this evening. I wish to outline briefly and in a general way why my Party and I are opposing this legislation. Then I want to give an indication as to the type of amendments that we will bring forward during the committee stage.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Let's go ahead, then.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Hon. Member says that we should go ahead and do it. We will. One of the realities with this type of complex legislation-and in a great many ways I do not think the public really appreciates this-is that to understand what it does and then to find ways in which it can be approved takes time. A number of us have been working since eleven o'clock this morning with members of our staff going through the Bill to try to see what can be improved upon to make a bad deal a little bit better for the people whose livelihoods will be affected by it. I wish to remind Hon. Members that it is not the presidents of the railroads or the shareholders-and let's face it, we, the people of Canada, are the shareholders of one of the two major ones-but it is those men and women who work for the Canadian railroads whose whole existence will be affected by this legislation. It will affect their ability to bargain. It will affect their ability to achieve a settlement that is fair. Once this legislation is passed and those people are sent back to work, whether it is tomorrow, Saturday or Sunday, it will be up to a nameless individual to decide on their fate for the next two years. It will be up to that individual to decide whether or not they will have a job, as a result of the type of policies he or she allows the rail companies to put into place with respect to job security, contracting out and technological changes.
August 27, 1987

We in this Party believe in the principle that the worker has to have a say in matters that affect him or her on the job. It is something which affects them as workers and, of course, it affects their families.
1 wish to deal now with the crux of the matter. We heard part of it in the exchange between my colleague, the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy), and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie). The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) well knows, because of our debates in the House over Freedom to Move, deregulation, and specifically Bills C-18 and C-19, that our profound belief is that a move to a free market system in transportation can only lead to the elimination of vast numbers of jobs within the rail sector. In effect, what will happen is that, as with contracting out, the Government will allow the theft of jobs from one sector to another, allow the elimination of jobs, jobs that are being held today by Canadian men and women, jobs which will not exist in the future.
Deregulation is at the heart of the problem we have before us today. It set the stage for the type of negotiations that the rail companies entered into with their worker representatives. It is fair to say that a great many jobs in the past were not due to deregulation. But it is also fair to say that much of the pressure on the companies is being brought about because of deregulation and the move to a free market system.
Let us remember that this is a very long country. We are not like the United States where everything is in a grid and there are people north, south, east and west. Here it is only east and west, by and large. It is the ribbons of steel that connect the oceans that are the hub, the dream, that have kept this country together. That dream is based on stability, a stability of service. It is one of the things the Government has forgotten about. Service must come first. The economics, although important, must play a secondary role.
I would now like to deal with the general concerns in the Bill. The Bill provides for a two-year imposed extension of the collective agreement, with the arbitrator given an opportunity, or the permission, to extend it to three-years. It is our understanding that at no time during the negotiations was there a three-year contract discussed. Both sides, company and union, were talking two years. We think there is no reason whatsoever that the arbitrator, this sole individual, should be able to add another year on to a collective agreement that has not been achieved through fair collective bargaining but has been imposed upon both sides by an individual who is not the choice of either side but is the choice of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux).
The question of contracting out-in effect, a process that allows a company to take a full-time, well-paying job from an existing employee and give it to someone else's employee-is job stealing. That is what we call it. I can understand the unions, not just in the railway industry but in all other sectors, fighting this type of clause. It undermines our whole fabric. It undermines the consumers who buy goods and food to put on
Maintenance of Railway Operations
the table for their families. I think that it would be better for the economy if we could retain these jobs within the rail sector, within the unionized sector, to ensure that the money that is needed in our economy continues to circulate.
This ties in with employment security. Hon. Members will note that I said "employment security" and not "job security". There is a difference. What the unions are arguing for is not job security in which an individual keeps the same job throughout his or her career but employment security in which an individual is assured of ongoing employment within the company. Workers are already being required to change jobs and to change locations frequently as companies continue to try to reduce their workforce. There is almost no one now working for the railroads who has not been there for at least eight years.
There are also concerns over centralization. A few years ago the CNR closed the bunkhouses in Atikokan and offered relocation to some of the employees to Winnipeg, which is 200 or 300 miles to the west. House prices in Winnipeg are a great deal different from those in Atikokan. If one is a 50 or 55-year-old married man who owns his own home in Atikokan and finds himself having no choice but to relocate, what he was making in Atikokan can no longer provide him the same type of lifestyle that he would be able to achieve in Winnipeg. The unions are legitimately concerned about the impact of those types of decisions on the people whom they represent.
One of the other items in the Bill is the question of the responsibility of the arbitrator. Basically, the arbitrator has a blank cheque. During the clause by clause debate, we may hear from the Minister on the intentions of his Ministry in regard to instructions to the arbitrator. Clearly, from the manner in which the Bill is written, it is a blank cheque. The arbitrator can decide on what he wishes to deal with which is in dispute, and perhaps ignore the key elements that either side may wish discussed.
In our amendments, we are proposing that we give the arbitrator a shopping list. This is not a unique occurrence; it has happened in other legislation which dealt with back to work matters.
A Bill passed in the first session of the 29th Parliament in 1973 dealt with a work stoppage on the railroad. That Bill included components, it established base increases in wages and criteria which the arbitrator, Mr. Emmett Hall, had to consider.
We are proposing that incorporated into this Bill there be a 4 per cent wage increase effective January 1, 1987. This leaves the second year of the imposed collective agreement to the arbitrator to work out with the two parties. This would ensure that those workers who have been without a collective agreement for some time will have the benefit of a moderate increase in their pay cheques sooner rather than later.

August 27, 1987
Maintenance of Railway Operations
We will also recommend that a list of the key items determined by the parties be included in the Bill, but not necessarily limited to them. I wish to state briefly the types of things that we want to say to the arbitrator through legislation that he must consider and deal with.
The arbitrator must deal with wages, starting rate for new employees, dental plan for new employees, extended vision health care for new employees, shift differentials, medicare allowance, job security benefits, employment security, contracting out, incidental work rules, yard switching limits, coupling-uncoupling hoses, disability pensions, dental plan, extended health care, and vacation. We are not limiting the arbitrator to those issues, because there may be other items that both sides feel it is important to resolve. We want to say to the arbitrator, "This is your starting list. You must not overlook these points because they are deemed to be important to the conclusion of the arbitration and any negotiations that take place".
We also wish to lift a section out of the 1973 legislation which states that the arbitrator shall closely examine the job security demands of the union, and fully explore the feasibility of a job security plan based on the principles of attrition.
In that amendment, we are saying that the Bill should have built into it the principle that no individual will lose his or her employment except through attrition. This means, within the terms of the collective agreement, when that individual is ready to retire voluntarily, or leave the workforce. There will not be massive eliminations of jobs, and massive permanent lay-offs of individuals. We did not dream that up. It is in legislation previously enacted by the House several years ago in a matter relating to a work stoppage in the rail industry.
Another amendment that we will put forward deals with an interpretation of the instructions in the legislation to the companies and the unions. There is a section which states, "every employee shall when so required forthwith resume the duties of that employee's employment with the railway company".
We are concerned that any of the railroads may use that particular wording to delay calling workers back for their legitimate shifts, or not calling them back at all. We recognize that this legislation will probably clear both Houses before tomorrow, so we are probably talking about a weekend startup. We understand that the office workers at CN or CP who normally work Monday through Friday will not have to be called back in for Saturday morning, unless there is a legitimate reason to clean up the backlog. We are concerned that the railways will use that particular wording to eliminate jobs, and we want to avoid that situation. We will move the deletion of "when so required".
I have mentioned the two-year contract as opposed to the third-year option. This is a minor wording of a technical nature. It states that collective agreements are between a union and a company. They are not between a company and an employee. A union acts as the agent of the employee through
legislation approved by this House. It is designed to protect individual workers in order that they do not find themselves in a position of having to negotiate on an individual basis with their employer, and be subject to all of the whims and other things that we have previously talked about. We are proposing that this be changed so that it is clear that it is between the union and the company, and not the employee.
I come from a transportation town where many railroaders live and work. As the House is aware, many of my constituents work in the grain handling and woods industries. Those industries are interrelated. I do not feel that 1 would be doing justice to my constituents if I did not stand up in the House and oppose this Bill.
What the Government has proposed is inappropriate. The parties should have been given more time. We could have worked with them. 1 wish to remind the Minister that this is the third labour dispute that he and I have dealt with in the transportation or grain handling sectors since I became a Member of Parliament in 1984. During the first two disputes he told me that there is a time when one should wait for the two parties to get things off their chest. He said this during the grain handlers' dispute in Thunder Bay, and he said it during the longshoremen's dispute in Vancouver. All of a sudden we do not have to wait these seven days. Bill Kelly was not whispering in his ear and saying, "Hang on, hang on. We have to wait a little longer".
During the discussion on the clauses perhaps the Minister may wish to respond to this. Why is there a difference in this dispute? The parties have been at the table for a long time, they were close to an agreement, and although they broke off negotiations, perhaps they knew that the inevitable would happen. The Minister had been saying, "If you do not get a settlement, we will legislate you back to work". The Minister also said that during the dispute in Thunder Bay. A settlement was reached. It seems that now there is a different set of rules for a national rail strike. I agree that it hurts the economy. More important, I think we have to recognize that unfair treatment of workers by any employer hurts our society. These workers do not want the moon. They just want a fair deal. 1 would urge the Minister to give due consideration to the amendments to see if he can incorporate at least some of our thoughts and principles. Perhaps the wording we have come up with is not as clear as we would like to have it or as is legally appropriate.

Madam Chairman, I have an amendment to this clause.

I would like to propose the following amendment:
That Bill C-85 be amended at page 2 by striking out lines 21 to 24 and
substituting the following therefor:
b) Every employee shall forthwith resume the duties of that employee's employment with a railway company.
The purpose of the amendment is very simple. It is to remove three words which appear in the current legislation. The three words are "when so required". It is quite clear on reading the legislation, and a number of employees have seen in these three words the possibility that the railways will never require them or might wait a long time before requiring them. I do not think that is fair. I think, frankly, that as soon as the legislation is to come into force, each railway shall forthwith resume operation of the railway, and every employee shall forthwith resume the duties of the employee's employment. However, to put these words "when so required" creates a certain situation. As one reads the clause, the clause deals with the responsibilities of the railways, on the one hand, to resume their operations and the responsibility of the employees, on the other hand, to resume their work. By putting in the words "when so required" in relation to the employees, we take away from them their decision to obey the law and we put the conditions for them to go back to work not on their decision, but on the decision of the employers.
I certainly appreciate the fear of some employees. In fact, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys, was speaking earlier in the House and addressed this very question. He received a phone call in the lobby of the Liberal Opposition from Mr. Steve Jursina, who is the local Chairman of the Brotherhood of Maintenance and of Way Employees in Sydney, Nova Scotia. He was clearly saying, "You are quite right," . He insists on amending Clause 4 to take away these words. He said, "We would certainly be in an impossible position because while we might be willing and ready to go, we might not be required by the employers. Therefore, we might be two, three, four, five days, one week,
Maintenance of Railway Operations
two weeks at home waiting for the requirements of the companies".
This is unacceptable. I hope that the Minister will accept this amendment to clarify the legislation. This is certainly not what the Minister wants. I do not think the Minister wants to leave to the discretion of the railways the time that the employees shall resume work. I believe the intention of the legislation is to ensure that when this Bill comes into force the railways will resume their operations and the employees will resume their work. Please, make it abundantly clear.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I also wish to speak to this amendment. We have a similar amendment which would have the same effect which we would have moved if the Hon. Member for Papineau had not introduced his. We see this as an example of two things. First, it is like the amendment that the Minister just made. It is one of the dangers of passing legislation quickly in that an effect which people do not imagine being created can be created. Had there not been someone who caught on to the fact that the previous amendment by the Minister was necessary, we could have passed legislation which would have been very faulty indeed.
In this case we run the same risk. We are giving to the railways the power to call back people when they require them. It does not mention in the clause that they will be called back when they should be called back. It says "when required". There is no definition or explanation. It gives the power to CN and to CP to say: "Well, we are going to call back 8,000 people next week, another 2,000 the week after that, and perhaps we will never call back George".
As I mentioned in my speech on second reading, this clause was not in place in the 1973 legislation. It is strange that a clause of this nature has been thrown in, a clause which obviously gives complete and unlimited power to the railways to determine when someone is required to come back to work. I do not think the Minister can justify that. I am afraid that this is open to abuse and that there is no remedy in law for the Government to do anything if the railways decide not to call back people when they would normally be called back to work.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
What worries me to some extent is that one wrongly assumes that one of the parties will do something which normally is not be done.

It ensures that there will be no lay-offs and that if there are to be job reductions, they are done in a way that would not hurt any individual through the loss of a job. It ensures that it is done at a voluntary level, either by early retirement and early retirement buy-outs or through voluntary relocation of employment.
We believe that this clause is as important now as it was in 1973. Clearly the issue before the negotiators on both sides was that of employment security and job security. This clause would ensure legislative protection. It would not prevent the railways from further downsizing the workforce, I want to make that perfectly clear, but it would prevent massive layoffs.
We have heard estimates ranging from 5,000 to 10,000 people whose jobs in the rail industry will be eliminated. This clause would ensure an orderly reduction without hurting any individuals or their families.
Conservative Members voted for this amendment in 1973. I urge them to do the same today while in government as they did while in opposition in 1973. I urge them to put a clause in

I want to repeat for the benefit of the Minister of Labour that the wage issue is an important factor. This is especially true if you consider two collective agreemeents, one with VIA Rail employees which provided 3 per cent the first year and 3 per cent the second year, and the collective agreement with Ontario Northland Railways which also provided for a wage increase of 3 per cent the first year and 3 per cent the second year.
Now 1 don't think we can compare the situation at VIA Rail and Ontario Northland Railways with Canadian National and Canadian Pacific.
Although 3 per cent was acceptable in the case of VIA Rail because of the financial difficulties of that company, the same cannot be said today of Canadian National and Canadian Pacific.
I may remind the Minister that the 3 per cent that were approved for Ontario Northland Railways employees were only one aspect of a very generous package, since in addition to the three per cent, that is 3 per cent the first year and 3 per cent the second year, there was this new job security plan we have been talking about for nearly one hour, a plan that was approved by Ontario Northland Railways for its employees, and it is the kind of plan that CN and CP employees want as well.
Consequently, if we cannot make any progress on job security, these employees should at least receive some concessions with respect to salary levels.
In his report, Conciliation Commissioner Douglas Stanley was not very generous on the item of job security. He rejected the employees' demands, unfortunately, and said on page 35 of his report:
I recommend that the parties agree either immediately to trade-off
reductions in the years service to achieve job security for some or all of the
companies demands for greater flexibility, or that they agree to a process
Maintenance of Railway Operations
whereby this could be achieved on an individual bargaining unit basis during
the closed period in a staged process.

So on the most important item, which was about job security, Mr. Stanley was less than generous. As for the second most important item, and I am referring to wage demands, 1 hope that the arbitrator to be appointed by the Minister will at least be more sensitive, more aware of these important demands and that he will act accordingly.
However, to be sure that is the case, if the Minister could include in the Bill that at least for the first year, the increase would be four per cent, at least part of the battle will be won.

I rise in support of this amendment. I wish to remind the Minister and Members on the government side of what the CNR wishes to do to its workers. On the one hand, it makes it clear that what it would like to do as quickly as possible is to reduce its workforce by 25 per cent in a very few years. On the other hand, it says to those who will be lucky enough to stay on that it does not want them to accept a wage increase of 1 per cent, or whatever increase is finally dragged out of it kicking and screaming, but it wants them to take a cut in wages. There is an increase in the cost of living of approximately 4 per cent, which means that the real value of the wages and salaries of the employees have been reduced by that amount. In addition, the company wants to impose a further reduction in wages on the employee.
1 ask Members of the House if the management of CNR. after these failed negotiations, and after the arbitrator looks into the matter and makes a finding, can expect to have a happy, co-operative workforce?
I saw back-benchers of the Conservative Party laughing when my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill, talked about the workers in Japan. Until a year ago when the situation changed dramatically, for reasons that we do not have time to discuss, the workers in Japan were involved in a highly productive society. In comparison with workers in North America, both here and in the United States, among the large employers in Japan, comparable to CP and CN, when a worker got a job at that company in Japan he or she had a job for his or her entire working life. If the company wanted to bring in new machines, computers, or automation, of course the workers did not worry because they knew that they had a job for life. The worker would co-operate and was willing to accept any new techniques or new processes. In fact, the worker was probably suggesting new ways to do the job faster and more efficiently because they were part of a team in which both the employer and the employee benefited.
The Hon. Member for Papineau referred to the management of the CNR as being rude to its employees. I was not there, so I do not know if they were rude to their employees,

but they certainly have displayed an aggressiveness, a toughness, and a "we don't care about you" attitude which is certainly new in the entire history of the CNR.
I would ask the Government to give some serious and favourable consideration to this amendment proposed by my colleague. If we put that amendment into this Bill which we are passing, it would say to the workers of the two railways that the Government and Parliament cares about them. It understands the difficulties through which they are living. It is sympathetic and wants them to do as well as can be done. Therefore, it says in the legislation that it is ordering them back to work because the country cannot live with an extended work stoppage, but in ordering them back to work it is guaranteeing a wage increase which will as least meet part of the increase in the cost of living which they, and everybody else in Canada, have to live through.

I have recently taken the opportunity to review some of Hansard during the last time that Parliament was faced with a similar situation, making a comparison to the arguments being offered by the Conservative Government today about the inappropriateness of the NDP's suggestions that the arbitrator be given instructions, and that some income protection be built into the back to work legislation. I would like to refer, if I might, to the remarks of the Hon. Mr. Stanfield, Leader of the Conservative Party, when he spoke in the House on August 31, 1973. At page 6109 of Hansard we find:
On the matter of wages, we are not negotiating an agreement but, rather, back to work terms as the Hon. Member for St. John's East emphasized yesterday. He expressed the principle that governs the amendments we will propose. That principle involves building into the Bill a protection to ensure that any settlement adequately takes into account increases in the cost of living as they can be more realistically projected since the time the Members of the Conciliation Board drafted their reports earlier this year. In imposing a settlement, this parliament can do nothing less than provide that kind of insurance.
Those words are from the former Leader of the Conservative Party, Madam Chairman. I do not know why the passage of 14 years should obliterate matters of principle in the minds of Progressive Conservatives unless there are no principles there to obliterate in the first place. Mr. Stanfield went on to say:
-Parliament cannot simply pass the buck to the parties in the dispute, or to a mediator or arbitrator, without some clear expression and direction of the matters for which Parliament is responsible-
As reported on page 6110 of Hansard he went on to say:
I emphasize that such action could in no way be construed as taking sides or attempting to make a final settlement judgment here in parliament. This would simply be Parliament, in this case, accepting its responsibility in regard to the extraordinary cost of living situation which now prevails in the country.
Mr. Stanfield was arguing that Parliament has certain responsibilities which have to be lived up to. He went on to say
in wrapping up, just before the then Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre spoke:
We feel these proposals would have a salutary effect on the employees concerned. Surely this is a very important consideration both in ensuring an orderly return to work and setting the stage for ongoing negotiations. We believe that Parliament would be doing no more than it should, in line with its limited role at this time, in supporting our amendments. We also believe that in doing so it will be doing what it indeed must do in the interests of justice in imposing a settlement at this time.
Those words were the words of the Leader of the Official Opposition at that time. I hope that this will at least put to rest, if not bring the Government on side, the notion which has been bandied about here on occasion today that what we are suggesting be done in the course of passing this back to work legislation is somehow inappropriate or irresponsible. A railway company or union that contravenes any provision of this Fart is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction and is liable, for each day or part of a day during which the offence continues, to a fine of not less than $20,000 or more than $100,000.
That may seem equal to some people. But when you take a look at who the people involved are, you see CN, a multibillion dollar operation, and CP in the same type of a situation. Some of the unions involved in the railways have a thousand members who would be facing a fine in the same amount as CP and CN would receive. It would be the same amount as the fine CN would receive. In every other case in which we have passed legislation, we have recognized that the size of the fine should have some relationship to the ability to pay. I think it is unfortunate that the Government did not recognize these variations.
In speaking against this clause, I hope that the Government will recognize that it is inequitable. I recognize that it is not willing to change this at the present time, but I would hope that in future labour legislation, we ensure that fines are equivalent to sizes of organizations being fined so that we do not impose a very heavy fine on small groups and a fine on CP and CN that would be completely insignificant.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, during my closing remarks on this legislation, I want to say that it is sad when Parliament must deal with back to work legislation. Certainly, the ideal situation would have been for the parties to negotiate a collective agreement. Unfortunately, it seems that it was impossible to arrive at a negotiated settlement.
The companies believe they must go through massive reductions in their operating costs and therefore are not in a mood to give generous wage settlements to their employees. Therefore, the bargaining process was jeopardized from the beginning because of this situation. Clearly, while under normal circumstances a collective agreement could have been reached, it was impossible to do so this time.
1 must say that for a number of years collective agreements have been reached easily in the rail industry. In fact, the last time that back to work legislation was introduced was in 1973. There have been good labour relations in the railway industry for 15 years. It is sad to see that the situation has changed.
In discussions with union representatives, I have been told that there has been a very drastic change of attitude on the part of management in recent years. This is regrettable and I hope that it is a trend that will not continue.
Clearly, year after year in Canada a number of people working for Canadian National, Canadian Pacific and other railways have been able to earn a good living. The railways have been a very important factor in the development of our economy and an important source of good reliable employment. Therefore, it is sad that after so many years of good relations, many employees who have been working for 20 to 30 years with the company are now seeing a drastic change of attitude on the part of their employers in terms of their treatment and consideration and friendship. The new attitude is one of confrontation or indifference.
I believe it is very important for the arbitrator who is to be appointed by the Minister to realize the difficulties that now
Maintenance of Railway Operations
exist in terms of labour relations in the railway industry and to try to correct the situation.
I am not very optimistic about the future of the railway industry in Canada, in the deregulation environment. Despite this, I hope that at least in the beginning of this new deregulated environment the arbitrator will see fit to give employees a chance and provide them with a good collective agreement. Fundamentally, it will be on his shoulders to draft the entire collective agreement because the two parties have not agreed to anything so far. It will be a difficult task for the arbitrator and I hope the Minister is fortunate enough to find an able person to assume this responsibility. I wish him luck and hope that this collective agreement will be well received by both parties and, above all, while being an imposed settlement, will be perceived by both parties as a fair settlement.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my speech will not be as long as the one I gave at second reading, but I want to indicate that we are still in opposition to this legislation. During second reading we explained that we understood the need to have the railways running in this land.
Many of us are from western Canada, and that is the area of the country which is most affected by a rail strike in proportion to its population. However, we do believe that this legislation, as it was presented to Parliament, and even after the amendments made in the last number of hours in Committee of the Whole, is still flawed legislation. We are glad the Government agreed to and helped to draft an amendment which means that the arbitrator will not be able to act independently to impose a three-year collective agreement on the parties which for over a year were trying to negotiate a two-year collective agreement. I believe we did make some wording improvements in that area.
However, in many of the other areas about which we expressed concern at second reading, this legislation has not been improved. My colleague the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), quoted from the Hon. Robert Stanfield in 1973 with respect to the purpose of Parliament and its role when we introduce back to work legislation and how it is important for us to go beyond the structural step of ordering people back to work. We must also consider the times and realize there should be reasonable guidelines for the arbitrator.
This legislation refuses to deal in any way, shape or form with the responsibility which Parliament should have undertaken. As a result, workers and the companies have absolutely no idea of how the arbitrator is going to work. As I expressed at second reading, we cannot put blind faith in an arbitrator. 1 mentioned my own personal experience as a negotiator for teachers in Manitoba. We had an arbitrator who ruled against something both the school board and the teachers had agreed to. It seemed, in his mind, to be the right thing to do. The two parties to the agreement could not sign the final package

August 27, 1987
Maintenance of Railway Operations
because of some other differences. They both expressed their acceptance of the salary package. Yet the arbitrator decided to act differently. We, by passing this legislation at this moment are making that same mistake.
We know there are certain things which must be studied by the arbitrator, especially in the whole area of job security. We tried to get the Government to accept the same amendments the House of Commons accepted in 1973. The amendments passed into law in 1973 were accepted by John Diefenbaker and by Robert Stanfield, supported by the former Member for St. John's East, the Lieutenant Governor of that province at the present time. However, for some reason this new Conservative Government will not accept the same caring philosophy expressed by the Conservatives of 1973.
The Government recognizes that arbitration can be a very long process because it has pushed for the possibility of a three-year collective agreement solely on the basis that the arbitration process may take a very long time. To compensate for something all parties recognize, we said there should be some salary adjustment which should take place for the first year of the collective agreement. Let the two parties work on the second and possibly the third year of the collective agreement. If they cannot resolve that, the arbitrator will deal with it. However, for the first year there should be some recognition for the workers who are obviously trying to make a living. With the price of goods going up across the land and with taxes going up at both the provincial and federal levels, those people have extra expenses. Those expenses are occurring now. If it takes a year or a year and a half for the collective agreement to be settled by the arbitrator, those people will be out of money for a very long time indeed. So we tried to move in that area in the last few hours.
We quoted Mr. Stanfield again, and the Conservatives, who in 1973 were in favour of recognizing a cost of living increase for the workers, would not do so now. I should point out that in 1973, the Conservatives not only supported the Liberal back to work legislation, which gave a salary increase, but the Conservatives moved an amendment to increase the salary. Not only did they accept the cost of living clause put in the legislation by the Government, but the Conservatives, supported by their leader, moved an amendment to increase the salary above and beyond what the government of the day wanted to give to the workers.
The New Democrats of that day supported that motion and the motion carried. So we had a motion by the Conservatives in opposition, supported by the New Democrats in opposition, and the motion carried. I find it more than passing strange that this new Conservative Government will not do the courageous thing they were willing to do in 1973. I heard one of the Conservatives say it was a minority government. Even if it was a minority government, what the Conservatives believed then, they should believe now. It is the same principle. The workers and their families will face extra expenses as taxes go up, as the price of food goes up and as other costs go up, and if
the Conservative Party in 1973 thought we should recognize that in the legislation, the same principle should apply today.
We are also concerned that we do not know who the arbitrator is. We wish the Minister had taken advantage of the advice we gave him earlier today. We wish he had used the time he had to sit down and talk with both parties. He has now assured us he will at least consult with both parties before he appoints an arbitrator. I hope he does that in such a way that we do get someone who is not only acceptable to both parties but who does have a knowledge of the railway industry.
The clause that may be the sleeper in this legislation, the clause that may give us the most concern, is the clause which says that employees "when required" must return to work. It was one of the first clauses we debated earlier this evening. It created a very excited debate as people realized all of a sudden that again we were doing something different than was done in 1973. The 1973 legislation said that those workers who were on strike had to come back to work, those employers had to bring those people back to work. This legislation creates a new scenario. It creates a new loophole for those corporations which are admittedly trying to reduce their workforce. They have a new weapon now, a weapon given to them as a direct result of this legislation.
We challenged the Minister in the House of Commons in a clause by clause study that if the people in the Transcona shop are not called back, if the people in Kamloops, Thunder Bay, and Yorkton are not called back, and if CN or CP uses this clause as their reason for not calling those people back, the Minister's credibility is certainly in jeopardy. This is a new weapon which the Government is giving to CN and CP. Previous back to work legislation tried to re-establish the status quo, to treat both employees and employers in an equal manner, to get them back to work to provide service to the public. The exception that the Minister made tonight is a dangerous one. I believe that in the case of CN and CP, which companies are trying to reduce their workforces, and which companies have used every method they could possibly use to do so, if the collective agreement says it cannot lay off 50 people without giving a long notice, then they will lay off 49 people, and then another 49 x number of months later, followed by another 49 x number of months after that. That is the existing practice in the rail industry.
We have now given those two companies another weapon. 1 predict that in some circumstances they will be tempted to use it. It will be our position as members of the Opposition, and 1 hope that government Members will also be keeping an eye on CN and CP, that if we hear about people who are not brought back a week or two weeks from now when the work has obviously reached the level it was prior to the strike, we will go to the Minister and get this legislation changed.
August 27, 1987

speechtext:
Madam Speaker,
I do not intend to abuse for very long the patience of those who are still here.
1 make one last try with the Minister in regard to the question of the language of people returning to work when so required. The Minister cited an example of previous legislation in which that language was used. He said that he had no problems with it. However, I wonder if the Minister has reflected upon the fact that the legislation to which he referred when he was making his defence of the language was legislation that applied to people who would be returning to work through the auspices of a hiring hall and not in the way that people on the railroad will be returning to work. I ask the Minister to think about that point. The words "when so required" may have been adequate to the situation that existed when people were returning to work through a hiring hall, but it may not be adequate and may indeed create the type of new power about which the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) has spoken. This new power could be given to the railways as a result of the wording in the Bill.
Finally, I want to say that people in my family have worked on the railway ever since 1912 when my grandfather first came to Canada.
There are many in my family who still work for the railway. I want to tell you, Madam Speaker, and 1 hope that Hon. Members will listen, that something terrible is happening to the railroads. Something terrible is happening to a way of life in this country. Something terrible is happening to the traditional relationship between labour and management and the way of life that was associated with working at the railroad. The Bill that we have before us will not help. It has the potential to make matters incredibly worse.
I say for those who may want to think about it years down the road, that unless something very, very serious is done to correct certain trends which are in place, we will have on our hands the sort of railway equivalent of the chaos that we have had at the Post Office for so many years. So much bad feeling is being built up as a result of new attitudes being taken by management that we will soon be at the point of no return. We will soon be at the point at which there will be no more trust on which to rebuild any kind of productive relationship between labour and management and employees in the companies.
I do not take any delight in that. I am simply saying that that is where we are. If the Minister had taken some of the amendments seriously, he would have had an opportunity to take decisive action to arrest that slippery slope that the railways are on at the moment. Unfortunately, we have not been able to arrest that slide here this evening because the Government simply has not been willing to listen.

We feel that the loss to the economy of the country by prolonging this rail strike would be extremely damaging. We do not see that continuing negotiations and prolonging the rail strike will in any way influence the Government on what we feel should be in this Bill that is not in it already.
There has been mention made tonight about concerns with respect to job security. I say to the Minister that we are disappointed that he has not seen fit to put in the Bill a recommendation that the arbitrator consider this question very, very seriously. Not only is job security not uniform among the various railroads in the country, it is not uniform among various areas of Canadian National within a certain region. I refer to the Atlantic region. The benefits should be there. They should have been there for everyone in the railroads. However, that is not the case. I hope the Government will correct that.
I also suggest that, with respect to Clause 4 and comparable clauses in the Bill, the words "when so required", which the Government did not agree to delete, would be taken into consideration. We in this Party will be watching very, very carefully to assure ourselves that those who were working for the railroads prior to the strike will be getting back to work in their jobs immediately after the strike terminates. If there is a breach of faith by the railroads in this regard then we definitely want the Government to step in.
I hope that something has been served as far as the Government listening to these matters is concerned. As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Papineau, has stated, this is not

I did not wish to speak originally because I thought that we had all said what we had to say. I notice by certain repetitions that we had done so. Nevertheless, I would like to add that it is never with great joy that as Minister of Labour I introduce in the House back to work legislation. Unfortunately, it is the second time that I have had to do this, and I do not find any joy in it.
I still believe that our collective bargaining system is probably one of the best in the world. To attest to this fact, and the fact that the parties usually use it to come to an agreement, last year out of 11,000 collective agreements that were reached and signed in Canada, 94 per cent were reached without one single day of strike or lock-out. Obviously, our system works very well. I am proud of the system that we have which falls under the Canada Labour Code. We are always
there to provide the services of conciliation and mediation in order to assist the parties to achieve those agreements.
Unfortunately, in this instance it did not work. Because of the impact upon the public interest, and because of the stoppage of the most important transportation system in Canada, we indicated that we could not and would not tolerate such a work stoppage. We had to step in. It is never pleasant, but we had to do it. We did it, and hopefully we will not have to do it again.
